title: Division between Iraq’s Kurdish parties risks undermining Kurdistan region’s autonomy
author: jon.wallace
description:
Division between Iraq’s Kurdish parties risks undermining Kurdistan region’s autonomy Expert comment jon.wallace 28 October 2026

The KDP and PUK largely agree on Kurdish issues in Turkey, Iran and Syria. But division on how to govern at home could invite outside interference and undermine hard-won self-governance.

Two years after Iraq’s Kurdistan Region went to the polls to elect a new government, the KDP and the PUK – the region’s two largest parties – have still failed to reach an agreement to form the new government. A caretaker government, originally elected in September 2018, remains in charge.

This situation is taking the Kurdistan Region down a path of profound and possibly permanent division. Its longstanding partners in Europe and the US have grown frustrated with its latent dysfunction and are no longer willing to play referee. This leaves it more vulnerable to interference from regional powers who are better placed to adapt and can play a longer game.

The main impediment to moving forward is not petty disagreements between the two parties over ministerial positions, as is sometimes claimed. Instead, the impasse stems from the collapse of the 2006 Strategic Agreement between the KDP and the PUK. The parties no longer share the same basic vision for how the Kurdistan Region should operate. The formal and informal frameworks that bound the two parties together for the last two decades are no longer functioning.

Instead, the Kurdistan Region has effectively divided into two geographic areas that are controlled by one party or the other. The KDP is in charge in Erbil and Duhok governorates. The PUK is dominant in Sulaymaniyah and Halabja.

The two zones are not fully separate, as they were during the era of divided administrations between 1998 and 2005. But it is a cumbersome arrangement. State institutions and the security forces look to unelected party leaders for guidance, not Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) ministries. Reports indicate that rents are extracted from truckers and traders at checkpoints on the border between KDP and PUK areas.

Until now, the parties have maintained that the Kurdistan Region remains a cohesive entity despite the partisan divide. On 6 October, KRG Prime Minister Masrour Barzani called on the parties to reactivate Kurdistan’s Parliament, which has not had a substantive meeting in more than four years saying: ‘I don’t know what they are afraid of’.

Below the surface, however, bigger changes may be afoot.

Hear directly from the experts

Get nuanced insights from Chatham House experts on the issues shaping the global policy and geopolitical landscape.

Political leaders from the PUK have a more radical proposal: to devolve administrative and fiscal authority to governorates, mayors, and district directors. Some powers would be retained by the KRG and the Kurdistan Parliament. But most important decisions over everyday matters would be shifted to lower levels of governance. Proponents of the plan cite Switzerland’s cantons and the UAE’s emirates as inspiration. Better to get out of each other’s way, the argument goes, and disaggregate executive authority.

Given the outsized power wielded – exclusively and separately – by the two parties at the governorate and local levels, this change would formalize partisan control over governance within the Kurdistan Region’s two zones, representing the biggest constitutional change in a generation. 

And it would repudiate the key peacebuilding assumption following the Kurdish civil war: that strong, unitary, and shared institutions are needed to reinforce Kurdish self-government and autonomy. That it is even being considered reflects the depths to which relations between the KDP and the PUK have deteriorated.

Many parts of the plan are vague. How would it change the relationship between local authorities, the federal government, and the KRG? How will revenues be shared, if at all? How will decisions be made about key sectors like oil, gas, electricity, and trade?

For the moment this remains a PUK proposal, its prospects uncertain. The KDP opposes the plan – part of the reason there has been little progress in negotiations to form a government. Many Kurdish voters will oppose reinforcing the power of the ruling parties without any meaningful checks. And, while they are certainly disillusioned by their present circumstances, they are keenly aware of the risks the PUK plan would pose to the Kurdistan Region’s fragile constitutional position in Iraq.

Over the past five years, Iraq’s federal government has gradually eroded the KRG’s ability to manage its own political and economic affairs, enabled by the KDP and the PUK disunity. 

A bad time for division

The potential for a fracture inside the Kurdistan Region comes at an inopportune time geopolitically. The US–Iran War has created significant instability. Foreign partners are preoccupied with problems at home. And changing regional dynamics are seeing sovereign states reassert influence over non-state actors.

The US presence in the Kurdistan Region is less potent than in years past. It completed a military withdrawal at the end of September after twelve years as part of the international coalition fighting Islamic State. Diplomatic activity in Erbil – where the KRG is based – has been hampered for much of this year due to security concerns stemming from the US–Iran war.

American and European diplomats are discouraged by their inability to bring the KDP and the PUK together, despite restlessly encouraging them to form a government. This inability is a signal of the West’s flagging influence over top Kurdish leaders. That will only worsen if diplomats have to contend with empowered local officials that answer primarily to the KDP and the PUK leadership.

The Kurdistan Region’s immediate neighbours like Turkey and Iran are much better placed to adapt to a Kurdistan Region that is divided and disaggregated. They can play the long game, and act at the local level through economic, social, and religious ties, rather than the top-down military and political approach of the US and Europe. Unity between the KDP and the PUK matters far less in their calculations.

Turkey’s immediate aim in the Kurdistan Region is to ensure that its own Kurdish political process, which is seeing the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) disarm, continues. The KDP and the PUK have strongly supported this process and provided important interventions to facilitate it. They have also supported the integration process of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) into the new Syrian state. 

In the near-term, the KDP and the PUK are unlikely to diverge much from this path. But the risk is that greater division at home could fragment their positions on issues beyond the Kurdistan Region’s borders. If that happens, Ankara might side with one of the parties, which would result in further instability.

Iran’s first goal is to ensure that Kurdish groups do not enter its war with the US. So far, the KDP and the PUK are in lockstep about the importance of avoiding any impression that they might intervene against Iran. Tehran’s second goal is to curtail the activities of its own Kurdish armed groups, even to the point of demanding they be expelled from Iraq’s Kurdistan Region. Weak and divided state institutions in the KRG make this difficult to achieve. That, in turn, makes it more likely that Iran will take matters into its own hands.

In the absence of a US security presence, interference from regional neighbours could also lead Iraqi leaders in Baghdad to become more hands-on in dealing with matters in the Kurdistan Region. This would be a bad outcome for Kurdish self-governance and would likely inflame political tensions between the KDP and the PUK.

The sour mood that prevailed in the Kurdistan Region during the election two years ago has only deepened. Pushing governance decisions to the local level in an effort to avoid intractable partisan impasse at the top is one proposal. But it could have significant knock-on effects.  

A continued impasse between the KDP and the PUK risks setting off an irreversible decline for the frameworks that have enabled Kurdish self-governance for the past two decades. To get beyond this blockage, leaders from the KDP and the PUK must entertain imaginative solutions, but not ones that further divide, weaken its shared institutions or undermine democratic principles. Otherwise, it risks becoming a place that other actors pick apart at the expense of Kurdish autonomy.

title: France’s riots and mounting debt reveal a country in disarray ahead of pivotal presidential election
author: LToremark
description:
France’s riots and mounting debt reveal a country in disarray ahead of pivotal presidential election Expert comment LToremark 21 October 2026

France’s violent protests put further pressure on Macron’s already weak government, give Marine Le Pen fresh political ammunition – and offer a stark warning for Europe.

Only three weeks after the peaceful celebration of Pope Leo XIV’s visit, France offered an altogether different spectacle over the weekend: burning cars, looted shops, violent clashes with police and the historic town hall of Limoges engulfed in flames. 

The contrast between the two events is stark. But they may both point to something deeper: a profoundly divided society, facing a crisis of self-confidence, hoping to recover a sense of direction and purpose. Beneath France’s political anger lies an anxiety about the future, in a world increasingly shaped by algorithms and faceless technology. 

Although this anxiety is not unique to the country, the timing is particularly bad for France.

A hijacked social protest  

It all started with high-school students protesting deteriorating teaching conditions and staff shortages. University students soon joined them, followed by trade unions and veterans of the ‘yellow vests’ movement, as grievances expanded to encompass living costs and declining public services. 

By 17 October, some 550,000 people had demonstrated, according to the ministry of the interior; organizers claimed 800,000. In any case, it was one of the largest mobilizations since protests against the government’s pension reform bill in 2023, which has since been dropped.

Most participants protested peacefully, although some young demonstrators were severely injured in clashes with police. Their demands were also quickly overshadowed by rioters who looted shops, attacked police officers and set public buildings alight. The French government imposed a curfew in the most sensitive districts of Paris and other major cities, bracing for further escalation this coming weekend. 

Such violence is hardly unique to France. Milan also suffered protests and looting last weekend, and the Italian government has just passed new anti-riot laws. Britain too experienced widespread rioting as recently as the summer of 2024. But the timing is exceptionally damaging for France. Its public debt is approaching 119 per cent of GDP, while weak growth, a persistently high deficit (the fourth highest in the eurozone) and soaring borrowing costs have placed France’s public finances under mounting pressure (it has been subject of an excessive deficit procedure by the European Commission since 2024). Meanwhile, the parliamentary stalemate that followed President Emmanuel Macron’s ill-fated decision to dissolve the National Assembly in 2024 has made it almost impossible to restore financial discipline and has pushed France to the brink.  

Related work

Europe, Brazil and beyond: Is the populist wave gathering momentum?

With the public purse under such strain and the destruction caused by the riots projected to exceed €1.2 billion, the question of who will eventually foot the bill is politically extremely sensitive. A new riot insurance scheme, planned for 2027, could push up premiums for small shopkeepers. For those whose premises have been vandalized or looted, being made to shoulder the cost of public disorder (and criminal behaviour) risks deepening the sense of injustice and resentment that has helped fuel social unrest.

The images of disorder reinforce the impression of anarchy and a country without a clear political direction – if not a failing state. They spurred a bond sell-off, heightening pressure on the French debt even further. This could be seen by malign foreign powers as an opportunity for destabilization, although there is no clear established evidence at this stage that external actors interfered and fuelled the unrest. But former prime minister and presidential candidate Gabriel Attal’s proposal to allow temporary restrictions on social media platforms during riots illustrates the growing concern over their capacity to amplify violence and threaten public order. The Italian defence minister went a step further, openly declaring that the Milan riots were the result of a ‘hybrid war against the West’ waged via ‘TikTok, social media and YouTube’.

France’s political centre no longer holds

With the 2027 presidential election only six months away, the political stakes couldn’t be higher. Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, has already used the violence to strengthen her discourse on law and order, while hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon has sought to capitalize on the social anger to denounce institutionalized police violence and rally the left-leaning electorate. Their political projects differ profoundly, but both are taking advantage of the dissatisfaction with a political centre that has struggled to demonstrate that it can still deliver – or hold at all. In polls, the two leaders are still the favourites to reach the second round of the presidential election.

It is difficult to address France’s current predicament without drawing a parallel with Europe’s other major economy, Germany. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which won 20.8 per cent in the 2025 federal election, now polls at roughly 28–30 per cent. Germany, of course, has seen nothing comparable to France’s weekend of rioting, and the sources of discontent are not identical. Anger mostly stems from a deterioration of Germany’s industrial model in the face of rising energy costs, more restricted expert markets and growing competition from China, alongside disputes over immigration and the feeling of a loss of identity. But the French and the Germans are asking the same question: can established political parties still protect living standards and offer a credible future? The success of the National Rally and the AfD suggest they don’t think so.

Europe’s weakening social contract

Related work

The AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt marks a turning point for Germany – but perspective is important

These are signs of a broader European socio-political crisis, further highlighted by recent protests in several European countries. For decades, the continent’s social bargain rested on the expectation of growing prosperity, economic security and a better life for one’s children. That expectation has clearly weakened just as Europe faces intensified global competition and the prospect of AI transforming entire professions for which young people have spent years preparing. The sense of social demotion and purposelessness is becoming personal. France offers a graphic warning of the political risks when such anxiety isn’t properly addressed by governments, constrained by an ever-shrinking fiscal space.

But the risks are high for the European Union (EU) too. As political anger directed at national governments grows, pressure on EU institutions and the compromises on which European cooperation depends will likely mount as well. Le Pen has confirmed that she wouldn’t fear a confrontation with Brussels over the EU budget if elected president. And the AfD has repeatedly called for an end to the support for Ukraine, a reset of Germany’s relations with Russia and the normalization of economic relations with Moscow, especially on gas imports. At a moment when Europe needs to show a united front to bolster its defence, deter Russia and revive its competitiveness, further political fragmentation in Paris and Berlin would severely undermine the continent’s resilience.

During the May 1968 riots in France, Prime Minister Georges Pompidou was asked by journalists to summarize the mindset of President Charles de Gaulle. His reply: ‘reform yes, chaos no’. With only six months to go before his decade in power comes to an end, President Macron has little time left to ensure that his legacy won’t be summed up by the opposite: reform no, chaos yes.

title: After Trump’s Russian diesel deal, will Europe give Ukraine the support it needs?
author: jon.wallace
description:
After Trump’s Russian diesel deal, will Europe give Ukraine the support it needs?  Expert comment jon.wallace 14 October 2026

The new row between Washington and Kyiv must not distract Europe’s leaders from the urgent matter at hand: how to sustain Ukraine’s economy through the winter.

An intervention by President Donald Trump this week has once again created problems for Ukraine’s war effort. The president’s deal with Moscow, which could see millions of barrels of Russian diesel released to global markets, was condemned by Democrats and even some prominent Republicans in the US. Trump openly framed the deal as an effort to secure ‘Lower prices for Americans’ as midterm elections approach in November. 

It is uncertain that the deal will do much to swing votes back to the president’s party. But it has created another open dispute between Trump and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy – at precisely the moment when Ukraine needs renewed, focussed support from its allies.

A mounting Russian assault

Recent weeks have seen a noticeable shift in Russia’s war strategy. Some had expected Putin to order a new wave of mobilization and a renewed offensive in the Donbas. Instead, he has moved to intensify Russia’s ballistic missile and drone campaign, with the aim of breaking Ukraine’s economy. 

There has been a marked uptick in attacks on ports, grain storage and shipping, seemingly to block Ukrainian agricultural exports. Key bridges across the River Dnipro in Kyiv have been hit. So have railways across the country. And attacks have continued on Ukraine’s energy grid (despite the ‘energy ceasefire’ Trump claimed was part of his deal with Moscow), extending beyond generation to transmission infrastructure. Meanwhile, strikes on Ukraine’s steel plants have put five blast furnaces permanently out of action. Retail, warehousing and logistic hubs have also been targeted.  

Russia’s intention is to tip Ukraine’s economy back into recession, cause hardship, and erode the morale of Ukrainians. It may even hope to spark a new migration crisis out of the country.

Ukraine’s ask of its allies

Wreaking havoc on Ukraine’s budget, as GDP stagnates, revenues stall, and the budget deficit widens, will increase Ukraine’s needs and the financing ask it makes of its allies in Europe. 

Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape?

Join experts and policymakers at our Security and Defence Conference for candid analysis of today’s most pressing threats.

That is a serious problem. Ukraine was already warning of a $27 billion defence financing gap in 2026 and a budget financing shortfall of $32 billion in 2027. The problems are so acute that the IMF will likely stall further disbursements under Ukraine’s $7 billion Extended Financing Facility (EFF) unless the financing gap is closed or new financing assurances are provided. The intensification of Russian attacks on the Ukrainian economy will only increase Ukraine’s financing needs, as will an extended war.

Putin’s strategy is clear. He hopes to increase the costs of supporting Ukraine at a time when Europe’s public finances are in a parlous state, and the far right – generally opposed to funding Ukraine’s war effort – appears to be on the rise in some countries. With key elections looming, particularly in France next May, Putin hopes to present Ukraine’s cause as hopeless, unaffordable, and a drain on European taxpayers. 

How will EU leaders, gathering in Brussels for a two-day summit, respond?

Russian assets

Europe needs to be ambitious and creative in how it funds Ukraine. The message to Putin should be that, regardless of President Trump, Europe is in this for the long haul and will provide Ukraine with the financial bazooka it needs to win the war. 

To begin, the $90 billion Ukraine Support Loan (USL) agreed at the EU Council meeting in December 2025 could be increased. Better still would be to finally bite the bullet and seize the €210 billion of immobilized Russia Central Bank (CBR) assets in the EU (mostly in Belgium) and €25 billion in the UK. It should be an obvious move for Europe’s leaders to have Russia pay for this war rather than their own taxpayers. 

The Belgian government, which has resisted any attempt to seize assets, should not have a veto on European security. However, its concerns over shouldering all the liabilities for such a move should be taken on board, with the wider European community providing an indemnity for its legal risks.

First, the assets should be taken out of Belgium’s jurisdiction to a common EU managed Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV). The assets can then be sweated to generate a higher investment return to fund even bigger Extraordinary Revenue Arrangement-style facilities for Ukraine. 

Ultimately the security imperative should prevail over legal and economic arguments against seizing assets.

Shielding Ukraine

Urgent measures are also needed to insulate the Ukrainian economy from Russian attacks. Militarily, the obvious solutions would be to provide Ukraine with more and better air defences. But these are in short supply as a result of President Trump’s war with Iran.  

To compensate for the emerging gaps in air defence, new solutions on the financing front are needed. These should include providing funding to enable the speedy reconstruction of lost productive capacity, perhaps through public-private partnerships. Two initiatives on this latter account are currently in focus.

One is a first loss compensation scheme, meant to mitigate the risks to existing insurers. The current threat is that even the limited insurance available to Ukraine will be cut if the risks from war losses increase. 

But if the Ukrainian government and international donors offer to cover the first losses from attacks on Ukrainian productive assets, private insurers will be more likely to commit to provide insurance cover. This will ensure that funding is available to provide for the speedy reconstruction of key economic assets – factories, farms, energy assets, transport and logistics infrastructure.

Another initiative being pushed by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development is the extension of the existing Ukrainian Recovery and Reconstruction Guarantee Facility (URGF). This has been used to help insure agricultural exports out of Ukraine. But its cover is limited in size to €2million per shipment and €5 million per client. And it covers just 60 days transit, not storage, and is limited to ‘Free on Board’. That means that farmers are not covered while grains are in port or in storage, where Russia is now stepping up attacks. 

Grain exports earn between $10-11 billion annually for Ukraine. Donors have to make the financials of shipping from Ukrainian ports work again. That means helping the market find solutions. To start, the government of Ukraine and donors could increase the scale and scope of the URGF, perhaps to cover port terminal storage.   

A deal to force Russia back to the previous Black Sea shipping deal would still be the optimal solution to protect this trade, or perhaps some kind of NATO air or defensive cover for its shipping. 

Trump’s deal with Putin undermines Ukraine, but it will not fundamentally change the war situation. What will be decisive is ensuring Ukraine’s economy gets through a difficult winter, so that the country can survive the war and ensure European security in the process. As the US becomes ever more unpredictable, European leadership is needed to bring this about. Will Europe step up?

title: The Yemen war is not just Saudi Arabia’s problem. It’s the Gulf’s too
author: thilton.drupal
description:
The Yemen war is not just Saudi Arabia’s problem. It’s the Gulf’s too Expert comment thilton.drupal 14 October 2026

The renewed conflict in Yemen exposes the limits of Saudi Arabia’s military options and the vulnerabilities of the Gulf states. A unified Gulf Cooperation Council strategy on Yemen and a credible political settlement between Yemenis are needed.

The Yemen conflict has escalated significantly in recent weeks. Houthi strikes on airports in Riyadh, Abha and Dammam have killed at least 20 people and injured hundreds. Saudi oil infrastructure has also been attacked. Within Yemen, renewed fighting following a Houthi offensive around the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait has brought return to full-scale war. 

The escalation is an alarming reminder of the 2015 Saudi-led intervention in Yemen. This came after the Iran-backed Houthis seized the Yemeni capital Sanaa in September 2014 and ousted the internationally recognized government from power. More than a decade later, the Houthis remain entrenched and clearly emboldened, while Yemen’s government is fragmented. Prospects for a political settlement currently seem remote. 

Since the UN-brokered truce in April 2022, Saudi Arabia has sought to disengage militarily from Yemen and pursue a negotiated settlement with the Houthis. Talks gained momentum in 2023, but the Houthis’ involvement in the Gaza war, including attacks on Red Sea shipping and Israel, disrupted the political process. US president Donald Trump’s intensive bombing campaign against the Houthis led to a separate US-Houthi ceasefire in May 2025. But it did not advance solutions to the conflict in Yemen.

Difficult choices for Riyadh

Saudi Arabia now faces a difficult choice between flawed options.

The first option is military escalation through renewed air strikes and an offensive by Yemeni government-aligned forces. But this risks returning Riyadh to the costly, ill-planned and ill-conducted war it has spent years attempting to extricate itself from. 

The Houthis have learned that even limited strikes can impose disproportionate economic and political costs. This gives the group leverage that Saudi Arabia’s conventional military superiority has struggled to overcome.

Seeking to contain the Houthis has also proved insufficient. Although the relative calm following the 2022 truce reduced cross-border attacks, it allowed the Houthis to consolidate their territorial control and strengthen their military capabilities, only to attack Saudi Arabia again.

Negotiation remains the most favourable route towards a lasting settlement. But it faces a fundamental obstacle: the Houthis believe they are winning and have little incentive to compromise.

Nor can Riyadh simply outsource the conflict. The US faces the looming prospect of a renewed confrontation with Iran and is therefore unlikely to have much appetite for opening another front or supporting a prolonged military campaign in Yemen. Saudi Arabia’s defence pact with Turkey and Pakistan may strengthen deterrence and defensive capabilities, but it does not offer a solution to the Houthi threat or Yemen’s underlying political fragmentation.

Saudi Arabia cannot win this war alone, but neither can it outsource its resolution. The lesson of the past decade is that military pressure without a coherent political strategy will only reproduce the conditions that allowed the Houthis to consolidate their position.

A Gulf problem

Instead, a collective Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) response is needed. Yemen and the Houthis have become a collective Gulf security challenge. It would therefore be a mistake to continue treating Yemen primarily as a domestic conflict or a Saudi security problem. 

The attacks on Saudi airports have further demonstrated the vulnerability of critical infrastructure across the GCC to missiles, drones and other asymmetric threats. This exposure is not confined to Saudi Arabia. In January 2022, the Houthis launched attacks on Abu Dhabi’s oil facilities and airport, killing three people and injuring six. This threat is particularly concerning for the Gulf states as most of their economic diversification agendas depend on secure aviation, logistics, tourism, investment and a stable regional environment.

Attacks on Saudi transport infrastructure also threaten the wider Gulf by disrupting vital supply routes. The kingdom’s extensive land connections have become increasingly important and provided alternative supply routes for neighbouring GCC states while the Strait of Hormuz has been disrupted. 

Yemen’s economic collapse, water scarcity and demographic pressures also make its stability a long-term Gulf interest. 

The GCC must therefore move beyond expressing support for Saudi Arabia. It should pursue a coordinated strategy that creates a unified GCC agenda directed at strengthening Yemen’s government and establishing a credible political pathway to ending the conflict.

Gulf unity must go beyond condemnation

A collective Gulf response must begin by addressing the divisions that have undermined previous efforts in Yemen. Most importantly, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) must move beyond their damaging confrontation over southern Yemen in early 2026. Despite entering the 2015 intervention as allies, Riyadh and Abu Dhabi have increasingly pursued competing priorities and supported rival Yemeni factions.

Reconciliation requires more than expressions of solidarity following Houthi attacks. The UAE should reconsider its support for southern separatist ambitions and work towards a unified but decentralized Yemen that accommodates southern grievances and competing political interests.

Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, must reassess its dependence on established Yemeni partners, particularly the Islah Party, whose alleged Muslim Brotherhood connections have long generated Emirati opposition. Riyadh’s reliance on Islah-linked networks has narrowed its political options and contributed to divisions within the anti-Houthi camp.

Both countries must recognize that their competing relationships with Yemeni factions have weakened the very forces they seek to support. Without agreement on Yemen’s political future, renewed military coordination will achieve little.

Gulf coordination must also be matched by a serious reassessment of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

The Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), established in 2022 to replace former president Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi, was intended to unite competing anti-Houthi factions. Yet years of internal rivalries, weak governance, and limited institutional accountability, as well as alleged widespread corruption, have undermined its effectiveness.

Saudi Arabia should continue providing financial support to sustain basic services and prevent economic collapse in government-controlled areas. But this backing should go to the government and cabinet, not the PLC.  

The experience of the Hadi presidency serves as a clear warning that a decade of backing an ineffective leadership did little to strengthen the Yemeni state or reverse Houthi gains. Today, Riyadh cannot afford to repeat that mistake.

A more effective governance structure is essential not only to strengthen the position of anti-Houthi forces but also to provide a credible Yemeni counterpart in any future political settlement.  

Towards a larger Gulf–Yemeni settlement

Although Saudi-Emirati reconciliation is indispensable, a sustainable Gulf strategy must also involve Qatar and Oman.

Qatar should contribute to a more coherent Gulf political approach in Yemen, including through its media influence and relationships with Yemeni actors. Oman, meanwhile, should retain its role as a diplomatic intermediary. Muscat’s channels with the Houthis and preference for mediation make it particularly well placed to facilitate future negotiations without joining military operations.

Related work

Why the Houthis’ Red Sea power play makes Iran even stronger

The ultimate objective should be a Gulf-backed political settlement that preserves a unified but decentralized Yemen and accommodates its competing political constituencies. All factions, including the Houthis, should be able to participate, conditional on verifiable commitments to relinquish heavy weapons and accept a common political framework. This would require sustained Gulf diplomatic and financial support.

After more than a decade of war, the Houthis still control Sanaa, Yemen’s government remains weak and Gulf divisions continue to undermine efforts to end the conflict. Avoiding another prolonged war requires a common Gulf vision, investment in a functioning Yemeni government and a political settlement that addresses the causes of the conflict, rather than merely seeking to contain its consequences.

title: Pakistan’s Tariff Regime: Comparative Perspective
author: Jiawen Cui
description: Pakistan’s National Tariff Policy 2025–30 (NTP) sets out an ambitious programme to promote export-led growth through reforms of the import tariff structure. This is an independent comparative analysis to establish a consistent basis for comparing tariff structures, particularly the treatment of para-tariffs and provides an updated assessment that reflects Pakistan’s tariff reforms introduced in the fiscal year (FY) 2025–26 budget and recent changes in comparator countries, where data are available. The short analysis covers Pakistan and nine comparator countries as set out in the NTP: India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Thailand, Cambodia, Indonesia, Vietnam and Türkiye. It draws on the latest available international data, published research by reputable international institutions and, where necessary, OE calculations using internationally comparable statistics. Together, the analysis tests whether the data support the NTP’s characterisation of Pakistan’s tariff protection relative to the comparator economies.

title: The short- and long-run effects of railroads on Mexico–US migration
author: David Escamilla-Guerrero, Giovanni Peri
description: Large infrastructure investments, such as railroads, in migrant-sending countries can reduce emigration costs and increase local development, with ambiguous effects on net emigration rates. This column examines how the construction of Mexico’s railroad network between 1880 and 1910 shaped migration to the US over more than a century. Railroad access raised emigration rates to the US about fourfold in the early 1900s, mainly by allowing people to migrate in steps, which relaxed credit constraints on international migration. A century later, long after railroads became obsolete, locations with historical access to railroads send fewer migrants, but they still send them to the same US destination. Railroads created self-reinforcing migration corridors that outlasted the infrastructure itself.

title: Trust beyond face-to-face contact: AI and the future of finance
author: Charles Goodhart, Ly Hoang Vu
description: Every institution in modern finance exists to manufacture and maintain trust across society. This column argues that artificial intelligence poses new threats to trust which can fundamentally endanger the financial system. Deepfakes and voice cloning make it hard to verify identity or trust visual and audio evidence. A further threat is asymmetric understanding, where AI agents act on decision rules and representations of the world that humans cannot interpret or audit. Policy must adapt to preserve accountability, build resilience against AI-enabled fraud, and protect institutional trust.

title: Brazil’s Amazon rainforest is at risk if Bolsonaro wins – but its low-carbon economy is here to stay
author: LToremark
description:
Brazil’s Amazon rainforest is at risk if Bolsonaro wins – but its low-carbon economy is here to stay Expert comment LToremark 7 October 2026

If Flávio Bolsonaro wins Brazil’s presidential run-off, he will likely roll back Lula’s deforestation regulations. But the country’s low-carbon transition will be harder to reverse.

The outcome of the first round of Brazil’s presidential election has put President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and his main challenger Flávio Bolsonaro – son of former president Jair Bolsonaro – into a run-off at the end of October. The result itself is not surprising. But Bolsonaro’s stronger-than-expected advantage over Lula and the consolidation of a right-leaning Congress – particularly the Senate – is. If Bolsonaro becomes president, Brazil will join the right-wing wave sweeping across Latin America.

Related work

Brazil’s presidential election is more than just another polarized contest

This shift to the right will impact Brazil’s climate transition plans. A Bolsonaro presidency backed by a sympathetic Congress will have considerable power to weaken existing environmental protections. But that does not mean that Brazil’s entire climate transition would go into reverse.

Brazil’s climate agenda is often presented as a contest between environmental protection and economic development. The reality is more complicated. The important question is which parts of Brazil’s climate policy a president can change, which require congressional support, and where trade, investment and private-sector interests constrain political choices.

Brazil’s president has considerable executive power over environmental outcomes. The president appoints the leadership of environmental protection agencies such as the Brazilian Institute of Environment and Renewable Natural Resources (IBAMA), determines enforcement priorities and allocates budgets that can either strengthen or weaken environmental protection within months. 

But economic forces also set boundaries. Brazil is deeply dependent on agricultural and natural-resource exports, and increasingly on oil. At the same time, large flows of private and foreign investment are reinforcing renewable power, electricity transmission and distribution, electric vehicles and other low-carbon industries. 

This distinction reflects Brazil’s unusual emissions profile. Unlike many large emerging economies, two thirds of the country’s greenhouse emissions are linked to land-use change. Brazil’s energy system is relatively clean; renewables already provide around 87 per cent of its electricity. 

The Amazon is at risk if Bolsonaro wins

The greatest risk from a Bolsonaro victory is therefore likely to be land use and deforestation.

When Lula returned to office in 2023, his government restored environmental enforcement, agency capacity and satellite monitoring. Under environment minister Marina Silva, Amazon deforestation fell substantially. The latest annual PRODES, an official satellite monitoring system estimate put Amazon deforestation at 5,731 square kilometres in 2025, around half the 2022 level.

However, enforcement regulations are reversible by executive power if they are not complemented by policy packages that structurally change land-use practices. Transforming Brazil’s underlying land-use model requires cooperation with the country’s powerful agribusiness sector, which Marina Silva did not secure. Policy packages would have to move beyond policing towards land-tenure reform, traceability, rural-credit conditions, restoration of degraded land and incentives that make productivity gains more profitable than land clearing and expansion.

If Flávio Bolsonaro follows his father’s approach, he will likely reduce the enforcement capability and, with congressional support, further loosen environmental licensing and forest protection regulations like Brazil’s forest code. 

Renewable energy transformation is harder to reverse

A Bolsonaro government would have much less room to change Brazil’s renewable-energy trajectory. Brazil has structural advantages in hydropower, wind, solar and biofuels. These sectors are supported not only by climate policies but by competitive costs, growing electricity demand, existing infrastructure, private investment and powerful domestic industries. 

Biofuels, a sector that is broadly supported by Brazilian civil society and agribusiness, will continue to have a strategic role. Unlike in many European economies, Brazil’s ethanol and biodiesel industries combine climate objectives with agricultural, industrial and energy-security interests. Given the existing renewable assets, investments and private sector contracts in place – and Bolsonaro’s strong alignment with private sector interests – it would be harder for him to change policy direction in this area.

The importance of oil

Alongside its renewable energy transformation, Brazil has also become a major oil producer. The discovery and development of the offshore pre-salt oil reserves has made Brazil the 9th largest oil producer in the world and the largest in Latin America. It has attracted significant investment and is expanding production capability. In addition, the state-controlled oil company Petrobras is central in public finances at both federal and state level. In 2025, it paid R$277.6 billion in taxes, 7 per cent of Brazil’s total tax revenues. 

The continuing disruption around the Strait of Hormuz strengthens the strategic value of Atlantic Basin producers like Brazil, Guyana, Canada and the US. Bolsonaro’s alignment with Washington and other right-leaning Latin American producers could reinforce the formation a new axis of oil production in the Americas. This could lock Brazil further into the position of becoming a strategic producer globally.

Although both Lula and Bolsonaro would continue to enhance Brazil’s production capability, Bolsonaro would likely push harder for faster licensing, private investment and offshore exploration. In 2025, Petrobras was granted a highly controversial exploration licence in the Equatorial Margin, along the Foz do Amazonas River basin and have since discovered oil. There are concerns Bolsonaro would accelerate the licensing for further exploratory drilling in the Amazon region.

The China factor and impact of Brazil’s trade relationships 

Related work

The Climate Briefing: Climate change, energy and geopolitics

Brazil’s trade and investment relationships will limit both Lula and Bolsonaro’s manoeuvrability on climate actions. Even if Bolsonaro is politically aligned with Trump, there are economic interests that will limit his ability to track too closely with the US administration – particularly on China.

China is Brazil’s largest export market, accounting for roughly 28 per cent of Brazil’s exports. It bought almost 80 per cent of Brazilian soybean export volumes in 2025, 45 per cent of exported crude oil and is also a major buyer of Brazilian beef and iron ore. This gives Chinese demand considerable influence over the economics of Brazilian land use and resource production. 

China’s dominance limits the effectiveness of other trade partners’ environmental regulations, such as the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR). Although the EUDR can impose stringent traceability requirements on commodities entering the European market, it cannot by itself determine production practices across Brazilian supply chains. The regulation will only affect the portion of large Brazilian exporters, commodity traders and banks that operate across multiple markets and therefore have commercial reasons to maintain traceability even if federal enforcement weakens. 

China’s importance also extends beyond trade. There are strong economic and investment interests between the two countries. The private sector in Brazil is not as suspicious of Chinese investment and technology as their American or European counterparts. In 2025, Brazil was the largest recipient of Chinese investment, with $6.1 billion invested primarily in renewable energy, clean technology and mining, further consolidating their strategic global positioning in renewable supply. 

Although Brazil’s current climate ambitions would be undermined if Bolsonaro wins October’s run-off, not all would be lost. The future of the Amazon rainforest is most at risk and the most vulnerable part of the country’s climate agenda. Brazil’s energy transition, however, is likely to progress regardless of who wins.

title: Russia’s Kaliningrad threats show the value of Baltic preparedness
author: jon.wallace
description:
Russia’s Kaliningrad threats show the value of Baltic preparedness Expert comment jon.wallace 7 October 2026

Moscow’s nuclear rhetoric should be taken seriously. But Baltic states know grey zone attacks and territorial incursions are equally serious threats.

Vladimir Putin always chooses his words carefully. If Russia faced a direct attack on Kaliningrad (its enclave on the Baltic Sea), he warned on 1 October, the use of ‘all weapons in (our) country’s arsenal’ would inevitably be on the table. 

The statement followed an earlier Russian note to NATO, threatening nuclear escalation if the alliance were to isolate Kaliningrad. NATO, thus far, has responded with restraint. Secretary General Mark Rutte said there was no imminent Russian threat and rebuffed Moscow’s nuclear rhetoric. But this skirmishing has pushed Kaliningrad – and NATO’s Baltic borders with Russia – back into the spotlight. 

Kaliningrad is not just any territory for the Russians. At the Yalta and Potsdam conferences of 1945, Soviet leader Stalin asserted his claim to what was then known as Königsberg. It was, he said, necessary for Russia to have at least ‘one ice-free port’ at the expense of Germany. The US and UK consented, and Moscow gained a permanent military position on the Baltic Sea. 

After the collapse of the Soviet Union and the withdrawal of the Baltic states to become independent democracies, Kaliningrad’s geographical isolation from Russia became more apparent, creating one of the most peculiar pieces of land on the continent. Today the enclave hosts Russia’s Baltic Fleet, missile systems and combat aircraft. 

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the surrounding geopolitics has changed. Finland and Sweden are now part of NATO. Poland is rearming at unprecedented speed. And the military presence across the alliance’s north-eastern flank is much denser. Meanwhile, Lithuania may soon vote to lift a ban on hosting nuclear weapons on its territory – a move the Kremlin described on 6 October as ‘a step towards escalating tensions’.

Kaliningrad remains a key forward position for Russia. But its near-complete isolation, in the middle of a more coherent NATO Baltic presence, presents Moscow with a serious geostrategic and military challenge.

Denying Russia a quick victory

One glance at the map is enough to understand that Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have but little strategic depth. The three states depend heavily on the Suwałki corridor – a 65km strip of land between Kaliningrad and Belarus that connects Poland and Lithuania – for overland reinforcement. Reclaiming territory from an attacker would be an unlikely option for Baltic countries.

The only credible alternative is to make a Russian advance difficult from the beginning. ‘We have to start from the border and win from the first battles,’ Colonel Tarmo Kundla, commander of the Estonian First Brigade, recently declared.

That is the purpose of the Baltic Defence Line along the eastern border: bunkers, anti-tank obstacles and other defensive outposts. Estonia plans hundreds of squad-level bunkers. A permanently deployed German armoured brigade will become operational in Lithuania in 2027. And Finland now hosts a NATO Forward Land Force. Defence spending across the region has risen far beyond NATO’s old two-per-cent target to reach nearly 5.5 per cent in the case of Estonia.

The intention is clear. Russia must be deterred from any attempt to seize even a small amount of territory – a significant possibility if Russia were to test NATO resolve. 

Preparedness before the first bullet is shot

But Baltic defence measures are about more than spending commitments and defending their Russian borders. Baltics countries know that to deter Russia it is just as vital to stress test their critical infrastructure and train their societies to keep functioning if and when a crisis emerges. Indeed, there is a lot the rest of the continent could learn from Baltic states’ whole-of-society model, which seeks to prepare their entire populations for an era of high-threat risk. 

From Finland to Lithuania, this model consists of embedding all the layers of society in defence and preparedness strategies. This form of ‘comprehensive security’ is grounded in the belief that keeping the country functioning in a crisis is a shared responsibility of government, business, civil society and citizens. In this regard, the Baltics are the most strategically advanced in Europe.

Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have accelerated preparations for grey zone conflict of the kind in which Russia excels, including attacks on infrastructure. All three have disconnected their electricity systems from Russian and Belarusian networks, progressively synchronizing them with the continental grid since February 2025. In the meantime, NATO has increased protection of Baltic undersea infrastructure, following damaged cables and various incidences of suspected sabotage. 

Slowly learning

Europe’s larger military powers are awaking to the need to somehow follow the Baltic lead and prepare their societies for an enlarging spectrum of threats. Germany, which would serve as one of NATO’s main logistical hubs in any reinforcement of the Baltic region, saw much of its civil-defence architecture fall into disrepair after the fall of the Berlin Wall. 

Its shelter capacity, for instance, now covers only around 480,000 people. Last spring Berlin approved a new €10-billion civil-defence programme, including plans to convert underground car parks, tunnels and stations into emergency shelters – evidence of renewed political engagement.

France has tested its armed forces at scale in the Orion 26 high-intensity exercise, which brought together 12,500 troops, 24 allied nations and civilian institutions in a scenario ranging from hybrid attacks to large-scale conventional war. The UK has developed a 2026 resilience plan that explicitly acknowledges growing Russian sub-threshold attacks. And the government is considering a reserve-style home-defence force to protect critical infrastructure. 

These are important changes. But ‘E3’ countries are still struggling to jointly improve resilience in transport, healthcare, energy, and communications – even as the risk of an enemy trying to disrupt all of them at once grows.

NATO is moving to drive the task forward. Its newly released resilience baseline requirements ask governments to plan for large movements of populations alongside military deployments; to develop health systems that can function even in case of mass casualties; and to develop communications and transport networks that can continue supporting allied forces during high-intensity conflict. In the near future, these will become the pillars on which deterrence actually depends.

Baltic gaps

Still, resilience won’t be enough alone to vanquish an enemy attack on the region. Baltic air and missile defence remains rather thin considering the scale of Russia’s drone and missile arsenal. Reinforcements would still have to reach the region through corridors like the Suwałki gap. And Russia would seize any opportunity to disrupt such movements. Fundamentally, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania remain reliant on their larger allies’ ability to swiftly provide additional forces and air power in the event of a significant attack.

This makes Stalin’s ‘ice-free port’ of Kaliningrad more than an isolated flashpoint on the Baltic shores. Putin’s nuclear rhetoric deserves to be taken seriously. Russia revised its nuclear doctrine in 2024, explicitly broadening the circumstances in which Moscow could consider nuclear use. These include threats to its territorial integrity and attempts to isolate parts of the Russian territory. 

But the military geography surrounding the enclave has changed too. Once referred to as NATO’s most exposed flank, the Baltics have become much harder to intimidate, and harder still to overrun before NATO can respond. 

Related work

Poland could be Europe’s rising star on defence and security

Their experience also carries a wider lesson for Europe: strategic weight is not measured by size alone, even that of a nuclear arsenal. Agility, civil preparedness and political resolve have allowed small states, free and democratic since 1991, to alter the terms of deterrence at their border. 

They have shown Europe that resilience begins long before deterrence fails and that it can change the enemy’s calculation. Their measures will make any attack look potentially far slower and costlier than Moscow would once have believed. Perhaps most significantly after the blatant failure of Russian objectives in Ukraine, Baltic resilience makes overall success of a military attack look far less certain for Vladimir Putin.

title: After the RAF Fairford incident, the UK should develop its homeland defence forces
author: thilton.drupal
description:
After the RAF Fairford incident, the UK should develop its homeland defence forces Expert comment thilton.drupal 7 October 2026

The threat of hybrid attacks from Iran and Russia means the UK should develop a force dedicated to protecting its bases and infrastructure at home. Finland and Poland offer lessons.

The US’s withdrawal of its bombers from RAF Fairford, following a suspected terror plot against the base, has brought attention to how the UK defends its homeland military bases and other critical infrastructure.

The UK government has insisted RAF Fairford is safe following the arrest of five men near the base on 27 September. President Donald Trump said the US withdrew its bombers from the base because of an unspecified ‘threat’ to the base. 

The investigation into the incident is still ongoing. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that there are ‘strong indications that Iran played a part,’ which Iran’s embassy in London has rejected. In March, the UK approved a US request to use RAF Fairford for what it described as defensive strikes on Iran. Tehran responded that any base used for ‘aggression against Iranian territory’ would be a ‘legitimate target’ for its forces.

Bases such as Fairford have their own protection forces that guard the perimeter. But incidents like this highlight the need for the UK to improve its wider homeland defence forces in the face of sustained pressure from hostile actors such as Iran and Russia. 

While the UK has specialist counter-terrorism units that can respond to incidents, and its armed forces and reserves can be deployed domestically to aid civil authorities in a crisis, it lacks a specialist domestic-only force that could protect a wider range of sites for a longer period.

Response versus protection 

The Fairford incident is just one example of the various hybrid threats facing the UK. Alongside Iran, Russia in particular poses a major threat. The Cabinet Office recently announced it would brief the chief executives of UK critical national infrastructure providers and defence firms on the ‘enduring and significant threat’ from Russia. 

Danish intelligence has also warned that Russia could mount a limited military attack against a NATO member within months. Across Europe, states have attributed drone incursions, arson and sabotage to Russia.

Protecting domestic sites is different to identifying the perpetrators or deciding on retaliatory measures. These happen after an attack; protection must be in place before one. This requires forces built for protection, not just response – which is what some UK allies already have. 

Poland and Finland’s approaches

Poland and Finland have both taken a structural approach, creating forces whose primary purpose is the defence of their own territory. 

Established in 2017, Poland’s Territorial Defence Force is the fifth branch of its armed forces. Recruited locally and organized around a brigade in each province, it remains in its own province when Poland mobilizes its forces, rather than reinforcing the regular military. Its stated tasks include protecting critical national infrastructure. 

Related work

Russia’s Kaliningrad threats show the value of Baltic preparedness

Finland’s approach is broader. A permanent security committee coordinates preparedness across government, working from a list of key functions that the state must keep running in a crisis such as water, energy and transport. Military and civilian planning sits within a single framework rather than separate departments. The premise is that defending the home territory is a permanent task, rather than a contingency to be activated during a conflict.  

Neither of these two models directly transfers to the UK. Poland’s territorial force reflects its position bordering Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad. Finland’s rests on conscription and a political culture influenced by its long border with Russia. 

However, the principle beneath both examples is transferable: protecting home territory requires forces raised specifically for the task, not carved out of regular forces each time they are needed. 

The UK has currently not adopted this principle. It does not have a dedicated force assigned to protecting a wide set of UK sites for a long period. 

Architecture without dedicated forces 

The UK is not starting from scratch. 

The Cabinet Office runs the Home Defence Programme, a cross-government effort to align military and civilian planning for threats to the UK. The 2026 Resilience Action Plan implementation report said the programme was being accelerated, with updated crisis response protocols and a planned national home defence exercise in 2027. The Ministry of Defence (MOD) has a Director of Homeland Defence and Strategic Threats. Standing Joint Command is the MOD’s operational headquarters for UK resilience tasks. 

A report published in January by researchers at the University of Exeter set out what this architecture lacks. The report argues that home defence activity is fragmented; that no lead department holds a mandate with executive tasking authority and adequate resources; and that the UK is at a standing start while allies including Finland, Poland and the Baltic states are years ahead. Its recommendation of a designated lead department is a good starting point.

However, even if these recommendations were implemented, a mandate does not produce troops. The UK has a reserve force. But alongside maintaining the UK’s own defence and resilience, this force is also expected to contribute to NATO’s collective defence and can be deployed abroad. 

Relying on the same reservists for both tasks only works while these two demands do not arrive at the same time. UK land forces are designed on the assumption that they will be deployed abroad, rather than defend domestic sites. In a crisis on the European continent, the task of domestic protection would not disappear. It would compete with the demand for British land forces to be deployed elsewhere.

Three changes the UK should make

Three changes follow. The UK should base its approach on the Polish design principle. This means setting up new reserve sub-units with a purely domestic protective role, recruited and based locally. These new units would be positioned near the bases and critical national infrastructure most likely to attract attention, and not counted as reinforcements for deploying formations elsewhere.

The new units would not replace existing forces. Guard forces such as the MOD Police and the Military Provost Guard Service, along with the RAF Regiment for air bases, would remain responsible for perimeters and immediate site security. And specialist units would still respond to incidents. 

Instead, the new units would do what the existing forces are not designed to do: secure non-military critical infrastructure, cover the ground beyond the perimeters, and protect multiple locations during a period of heightened threat. They would be designed to hold these sites for periods of months rather than days. 

This does come at a cost. Every reservist given a home defence role is one fewer available for deployment, and that is a real reduction in what the UK can send abroad. But in a situation when both home defence and overseas demands occur, the choice of home defence will need to be prioritized by default. Making that choice deliberately now means the force is generated and ready before that happens. 

From Finland, the UK should take the treatment of homeland protection as a permanent function rather than a contingency. This means protecting a budget for it, since activity funded from training and readiness budgets is vulnerable when defence budgets are squeezed. The British Army has already reportedly been told to suspend major exercises this year for lack of funds, and in September it was reported that army reservists are set to serve fewer days because of budget cuts. 

Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape?

Join experts and policymakers at our Security and Defence Conference for candid analysis of today’s most pressing threats.

Finally, the UK’s distribution of its protective forces should follow from the government’s decisions and the threats those decisions potentially attract, rather than from isolated incidents. When the government permits an operation from British territory, as it did at Fairford, it should decide the protective requirements at the site and its surrounding areas at the same time. 

The UK has the intelligence capability and the legal framework to protect its domestic sites. It also has the beginnings of a coordinating structure, though it needs a clearer lead. What it now also needs is a dedicated force assigned to protecting those sites across the homeland.

title: Trump is set to redefine the lame duck presidency
author: jon.wallace
description:
Trump is set to redefine the lame duck presidency Expert comment jon.wallace 4 November 2026

Conventional wisdom says the Democrats in Congress will now constrain the president. Nobody told President Trump. 

Although Donald Trump’s name was not on any ballot this week, American voters viewed the 2026 midterm election cycle as a referendum on his presidency. With the votes counted the message Americans delivered to the president is clear: they do not approve. They don’t approve of the cost of petrol at the pump, they don’t approve of the state of the US economy, and they don’t approve of the war with Iran.

Having lost control of both congressional houses, conventional wisdom would dictate that the executive branch should be hampered for the remainder of Trump’s second term. But the president has never operated by the rules of conventional wisdom. 

We should not expect Trump to recede into the background. And this is not (yet) the end of the Trump era. Like so many facets of American politics over the past decade, Trump is set to redefine the lame duck presidency. With midterm elections behind him, the president can now (re)turn to what he cares about most: his legacy. 

A foregone electoral conclusion

It has been clear for months that Trump was resigned to the prospect that the midterms would not go well. Republicans hoped the president would demonstrate discipline on top issues for US voters: the economy, affordability, and the cost of living. Instead, he spent the run-up to the elections preoccupied elsewhere. 

He picked a fight with Canada that very few at home understood. He found no exit ramp for a conflict in the Middle East that has driven up global energy pricing and hit American pocketbooks. And he reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to purchase millions of tons of Russian diesel, ostensibly to ease the pressure valve on energy costs at home but in practice befuddling many. 

As a result, and to some extent due to Democratic party momentum, Republicans found themselves adrift for much of the midterm cycle.

The scope of congressional constraint

History and US political norms suggest that a divided government should constrain a president’s second term policy agenda. Both President George W. Bush and President Barack Obama saw their aspirations for immigration reform fall short during their final years, opposed by hostile congresses.  

President Trump has already had some experience with adversarial congressional dynamics. During his first term, his ambitions around border wall funding, infrastructure investment, and changes to the US immigration system failed to materialize, after Democrats regained control of the House of Representatives in the 2018 midterms. 

That experience informed the Project 2025 agenda that helped shape Trump’s second administration. The president re-entered office in January 2025 and adopted a flood the zone strategy, signing two dozen executive orders on his first day. 

The administration moved quickly to secure Republican-led congressional approval for Trump’s major legislative priorities including the One Big Beautiful Bill, the Laken Riley Act and the Secure America Act. But Trump’s plan was always to lean heavily on his executive authority, to rely only selectively on Congress, and to be undeterred by inevitable legal challenges. 

Over the course of his second term, the president has issued 292 executive orders, 90 memoranda and 192 proclamations. Much of his remaining domestic policy priorities – including on artificial intelligence, immigration, deregulation, and energy – will be funnelled through the president’s office in his final two years. 

Democrats know this. Now back in control of Congress, they intend to use their oversight authorities including power of the purse, approvals over presidential appointments and investigations to slow President Trump down. This approach has precedent – though the recent record is mixed. 

On the one hand, congressional Republicans successfully blocked Obama’s 2016 nomination of Merrick Garland to the Supreme Court. Likewise, during the second half of Joe Biden’s presidency, Republicans used debt ceiling negotiations to secure concessions on government spending. 

On the other hand, impeachment investigations during Trump’s first term expended a lot of congressional energy but ended with two Senate acquittals. Indeed, both the Trump and Clinton impeachment efforts demonstrated there are limits to the bite of congressional oversight. 

Congressional Democrats may pursue impeachment investigations again (including against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth). But they won’t have the two-thirds majority they need in the Senate to ensure a conviction. And recent polling suggests that Americans believe it will make no difference for the president or his agenda. In fact, a quarter of those polled believe that renewed impeachment efforts will embolden the president and make him more popular. They may be right.

Despite the best intentions of the founding fathers, the US political environment has shifted over the last decade. Extreme polarization has created a politics in which Americans no longer share facts, eroding the system of checks and balances. Politicians across the political spectrum are no longer working together. The likelihood that the next Congress will be able to achieve a veto-proof supermajority on any legislation remains minimal. And Trump has already made clear he intends to be Mr. Veto. 

Rather than constraining the president, the next Congress may therefore end up constraining itself. That will leave Trump to pursue the ambitions left on his to do list. 

The final countdown

Atop Trump’s agenda is his legacy. 

During his second term, the president has sought to remake the world in his image. He pursued a policy of ‘reciprocal’ tariffs and a global rebalancing on trade. He treated allies like Canada and Mexico as competitors and adversaries. He roiled global markets and European leadership with talk of taking over Greenland. He flattered China’s Xi Jinping and chastised Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Trump replaced ideology with transactionalism, and consultation with unilateralism.

With the days now winding down on his presidency, and so many moves on the global chessboard made, President Trump will now seek a memorable endgame. 

He has long hoped to pull a rabbit out of the hat in Ukraine. But brokering a lasting ceasefire in the conflict theatre has thus far eluded him. 

In his frustration, Trump’s preference has recently swung back in the direction of President Putin, much to Europe’s dismay. For Trump the war is about access, energy and critical mineral resources, and proximity to power. He will hope that next week’s planned trilateral meetings in Abu Dhabi offer a first step towards momentum to end the conflict under his stewardship. 

Trump is also desperate to manufacture a resolution to the deepening quagmire in Iran. Nearly nine months into an intended multiweek operation, the realities of a war that may alone have cost Republicans the midterms are not favourable. 

With diplomacy stalled and economic leverage taking time, there have been growing indicators in recent weeks that the US and Israel may soon renew military action. Regardless of this midterms result, that remains a real possibility. As it stands, Trump owns another war in the Middle East that threatens a frustrating or humiliating outcome. In his quest for victory, he will be tempted to give kinetic conflict another try.  

Historic recognition 

Speaking before America and the world at his second inauguration, Trump laid out his presidential vision: ‘My proudest legacy will be that of a peacemaker and unifier,’ he said. ‘That’s what I want to be: a peacemaker and a unifier’. 

However, Trump’s greatest goal is securing his legacy. That influenced his claims to have ‘successfully ended’ eight long-standing conflicts, his plans to erect monuments in Washington and remake the White House ballroom, his decision to go to war with Iran, and, of course, his desire to one day finally be recognized with the Nobel Peace Prize.

The president has every intention of realizing this legacy. He will not let inconveniences like domestic politics, divided government or the US political system constrain him. Trump intends to fly like a free bird, not sink like a lame duck.

title: After Orbán, Vučić falls: can Serbia’s students herald a new dawn for the Balkans?
author: sfarrell.drupal@chathamhouse.org
description:
After Orbán, Vučić falls: can Serbia’s students herald a new dawn for the Balkans? Expert comment sfarrell.drupa… 27 October 2026

The consequences of President Aleksandar Vučić’s departure are hard to predict. But the victory of the Student List in Serbia is a promise of change in a country that could be a driver of economic growth and political integration in the Balkans.

Six months after Viktor Orbán’s defeat in Hungary, another European strongman has fallen, conceding an election he expected to win, in a consequential turning point for the country and for Europe.

President Aleksandar Vučić, in power since 2012, called Serbia’s snap parliamentary vote after nearly two years of student protests, and admitted defeat on Sunday.

With almost all ballots counted, the Student List secured more than 53 per cent of the vote and around 140 seats in the 250-member parliament. Turnout approached a historic 70 per cent, the highest since Yugoslavia’s break-up in 1992.

For the second time this year, a European populist with what looked to many like an unassailable grip on power has recognised electoral defeat, paving the way for a peaceful transition. The consequences of Vučić’s departure, however, particularly with regard to Serbia’s relations with Europe and Russia, remain difficult to predict.

History was born in a railway station

How could the seemingly unshakable rule of Vučić be brought to a sudden end by a movement that barely existed two years ago? 

History is sometimes born in what looks politically unremarkable.

In 2024, the canopy of a recently renovated railway station collapsed in Novi Sad in northern Serbia, killing 16 people. Rather quickly what at first looked like a tragic accident became, for many, a case study in perceived corruption during the Vučić era - no matter how much the government denied accusations of favouritism and lack of transparency over contracts issued for earlier renovations.

The tragedy ignited a protest from students across Serbia. It did not take long for teachers, then farmers and ultimately ordinary citizens to join them. What began as a leaderless protest movement gradually developed into a formidable political organisation, becoming  a pole of attraction for anti-government voters.

The Studenti u blokadi (‘Student Blockade’) movement quickly combined mass demonstrations with grassroots campaigning, including in provincial communities long dominated by Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

The movement’s electoral list ‘Studentska lista-Studenti pobeđuju’ (‘Students’ List - Students Win’) brought together 250 candidates, including academics, doctors and artists, with cardiologist Ilija Srđanović at its helm.

Their defeat of Vučić brings an end to twelve years of his personal dominance as prime minister (2014-2017) and president (2017-2026).

European leaders who for years had more or less treated Vučić as a guarantor of stability in the Balkans  – even as Serbian democratic institutions deteriorated – will monitor the next developments very carefully. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos have already welcomed the result and offered support.

Moscow loses a political partner, but ties will remain

For the Kremlin, the result comes as another setback after Orbán. The circle of pro-Russians amongst European leaders is growing increasingly thin – Slovakia’s Fico the last man standing.

Vučić had cultivated close relations with Moscow for years, refused to join EU sanctions following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and benefited from Russian diplomatic support over Kosovo.

But his position was more ambiguous than Moscow’s public praise suggested. Under his rule, Serbia defended Ukraine’s territorial integrity, including Crimea, and provided Ukrainian forces with Serbian ammunition.

A change in that balancing-act policy appears unlikely. The Student List has explicitly ruled out sanctions against Moscow, pledged to preserve military neutrality and rejected NATO membership. On Monday, its representative Jovo Bakić reaffirmed that Serbia’s foreign policy towards Russia would remain unchanged. The Kremlin has also adopted a careful tone, signalling a wish to retain good relations with Belgrade.

Such caution from the student movement reflects political realism at a time when the geopolitics around the war in Ukraine is more uncertain than ever.

Russia supplies around 2.2 billion cubic metres of gas to Serbia annually at favourable prices. A renewal of the existing Russian gas agreement, which expires in December, cannot be excluded at this stage. Russian companies also hold a majority stake in NIS, which operates Serbia’s only oil refinery and plays a key role in securing the country’s petrol and diesel supplies.

It is also unlikely that the next government will ignore Moscow’s continued diplomatic backing over Kosovo. Moscow can also veto Kosovo’s admission to the United Nations, or abstain.

Given the popularity that Russia retains among parts of the Serbian electorate, it is easy to understand why the student movement has thus far shown reluctant to break with Moscow. That same realism could complicate Serbia’s prospects of joining the EU.

A new opening for Serbia’s EU accession talks?

Serbia’s EU accession process has been effectively stalled for almost five years. In July, eight member states blocked the opening of another negotiating cluster, citing democratic backsliding and insufficient alignment with European foreign policy.

In a process that could be compared with that in Hungary, the new government could restore the EU momentum through reforms of the judiciary, public procurement and media freedom.

The stumbling stone, however, would remain Belgrade’s refusal to join European sanctions against Russia. Kosovo would be another obstacle: the Student List firmly rejects its independence, while Brussels requires Belgrade to normalise relations with Pristina.

The movement’s caution doesn’t just reflect its political realism. It also stems from the diversity of its supporters. It is, after all, the nature of big-tent political movements to adopt a cautiously conservative stance on foreign policy, given the heterogeneity of their electorate. In the case of the students’ supporters: a mix of pro-European liberals and conservative nationalists united against Vučić, with little in common on foreign policy. However, surveys suggest that three-quarters of Student List supporters favour closer relations with the EU rather than Russia.

The most direct implications of a political renewal in Belgrade will be for the Balkan neighbourhood. In Bosnia we can foresee a withdrawal of the political support Vučić provided to the nationalist Milorad Dodik, former president of Republika Srpska. Relations with Montenegro could also improve.

None of those changes is guaranteed. But Serbia now has a historic opportunity to rebuild its standing in the region, provided its new leaders can agree on the direction of travel.

The harder test is yet to come: to govern

The Student List now faces an immediate paradox: what got them so far will only get them so far. Its decentralised organisation helped it grow from a local protest mobilisation into a massive national movement in only two years. Governing will demand something different: clearer leadership and collective discipline.

Yet most of the movement’s representatives have little experience of government and parliament - if any. The identity of the next prime minister is still unknown, although names have been circulating, such as former central bank governor Dejan Šoškić.

The parallel with Hungary is, again, interesting: the new government will have to confront entrenched networks of the outgoing ruling party within public institutions. The next few months will be crucial to sustain the political momentum, as presidential elections are due before the end of this year.

The next test, once a government has been formed, will be to maintain a stable parliamentary majority as the first difficult policy decisions arise.

Addressing student protesters against Slobodan Milošević in Belgrade in March 1991, Serbian literary giant Borislav Pekić reminded them that ‘the essential thing is not to watch the clock. Victories are not won in a second, or a day, or a year’.

Thirty-five years later, their successors have achieved what few thought possible: ending Vučić’s rule overnight. The challenge now will be to turn this electoral victory into lasting democratic change. Watching the clock will be essential.
