title: Foreign rivalries risk turning Somalia’s political crisis into a protracted war
author: thilton.drupal
description:
Foreign rivalries risk turning Somalia’s political crisis into a protracted war Expert comment thilton.drupal 15 October 2026

Somalia’s domestic instability is being compounded by sharpened regional rivalries, paving the way for a more entrenched conflict as seen elsewhere in the Horn of Africa.

Somalia has been embroiled in a political crisis since May 2026, when the term of President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud was originally due to expire. Parliament passed constitutional amendments in March that extended presidential terms to five years, keeping President Hassan Sheikh in office until May 2027. 

This was disputed by Somalia’s opposition alliance, a coalition of political figures including the leadership of the federal member states of Puntland in the north and Jubaland in the south, as well as the former president of South West State, Abdiaziz Laftagareen. This week, the opposition also rejected the electoral commission’s unilateral announcement that parliamentary and presidential polls would take place in April and May 2027.

The political crisis has sparked fierce clashes in Mogadishu and the city of Baidoa in South West State. The recent fighting around Baidoa, between government forces and opposition-allied fighters loyal to Laftagreen, reportedly involved thousands of fighters and the use of drones and fighter jets. 

The federal government, along with its allied federal member state administrations – South West, Hirshabelle, and Galmudug – controls most major cities in southern and central Somalia, while Jubaland, in the far south, is at odds with Mogadishu. Al-Shabaab, an al-Qaeda-affiliated organization, controls much of the surrounding countryside. Meanwhile, the administrations of Puntland and the self-declared Republic of Somaliland govern much of the north, with the newly created and federal government-aligned North East State squeezed in-between. 

High stakes amid regional tensions

This is not Somalia’s first experience of constitutional disputes leading to armed clashes, with similar conflict occurring in 2021. But the stakes are higher this time, as the balance of power within the federal system is at stake. The opposition accuses the current federal government under President Hassan Sheikh of seeking to consolidate power in Mogadishu at the expense of the states.

Related work

War has returned to Tigray. This time it may not stay in Ethiopia

The conflict in Somalia is also taking place in a region that has increasingly become the focus of escalating rivalries between foreign powers in a complex web of alliances. Two broad, fluid blocs have taken shape: Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Turkey are seen as broadly aligned with Sudan’s Armed Forces and Eritrea in the region, while the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Israel are seen as broadly aligned with Ethiopia. 

In Somalia’s current political crisis, Turkey and the UAE are the two most important external actors. Turkey is seen as backing the federal government, while the UAE has relations with the opposition state administrations. 

These dynamics are helping to both incentivize new alliances and deepen divisions. Given the existing domestic volatility, there is a serious compound risk of newly entrenched conflict. 

Turkey and the UAE

Turkey has been engaged in Somalia for over a decade, primarily but not exclusively through the federal government in Mogadishu. Its initial involvement concentrated on humanitarian and development initiatives. It has also run a military training camp for the Somali armed forces since 2017.

Turkey has drawn closer to the Hassan Sheikh administration since 2024 after signing several strategic agreements with Mogadishu. This prompted some opposition figures to question Turkey’s neutrality in the context of the current conflict over the presidential term extension. Turkey has rejected accusations of political interference and says its position is consistent with its support for Somalia’s federal government institutions. 

However, more recently, Turkish fighter jets were reportedly involved in the fighting near Baidoa. This has not been confirmed by Ankara, but would constitute a notable direct intervention against armed political opposition. 

The UAE established multi-layered ties with the current federal government and some of the country’s federal member states. However, in January 2026, Somalia’s federal government annulled all its defence and security cooperation agreements with the UAE, accusing it of undermining Somalia’s national sovereignty. 

This move coincided with the Saudi-Emirati rift in Yemen. Days before annulling the agreements, Somalia launched an investigation after the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen accused Abu Dhabi of facilitating the evacuation of a Yemeni separatist leader to the UAE via Berbera and Mogadishu. Somalia then signed defence agreements with Saudi Arabia and Qatar, with diplomatic support from Turkey and Egypt.

The UAE has maintained direct relations with Somaliland, Puntland and Jubaland, with Emirati firms maintaining significant interests in port operations. All of these regional administrations had rejected the cancellation of the agreements by Mogadishu. 

Retaining influence with the leadership in each territory is therefore critical to the UAE’s wider strategy in the Horn of Africa. But its relations with the federal states opposed to Mogadishu are contributing to further inflaming tensions.  

Domestic drivers 

Local actors are also increasingly looking outwards for foreign backing to shore up their domestic interests and legitimacy. To attract support, both the federal government and the opposition are making efforts to show that their domestic influence aligns with the interests of external actors. 

This appeal to foreign players is driven by multiple factors. Key among them is the profound political division among Somali political actors, and the persistent failure to genuinely address these divisions. To counterbalance their local political rivals, competing domestic elites are therefore seeking to offer strategic incentives to external powers such as port investments, economic partnerships, transport corridors and military bases.

The federal government’s controversial constitutional and electoral reforms have solidified these divisions. Some federal member states and Somaliland feel threatened by Mogadishu’s consolidation of power, backed by Turkey’s reported military support and investments. 

Shifting regional geopolitical dynamics are also increasing the leverage available to domestic actors in Somalia. The Houthis’ advance in Yemen has once again exposed the importance of the Bab al-Mandab Strait connecting the Gulf of Aden and the Red Sea, reinforcing Somalia’s strategic location. The Houthis reportedly have growing relations with al-Shabaab in Somalia.  

The risks of deepening war

Somalia has been embroiled in armed conflicts for over three decades. No single entity – whether a clan, a specific administration or a regional government – has been able to dominate the rest and rule the entire country. 

However, the escalation of current armed clashes between political opponents, and the involvement of more sophisticated weaponry, points to a new chapter. Local actors are increasingly seeking external support and new alliances as a counterbalance to rising threats. 

For example, a minister from Laftagareen’s former South West State administration recently stated that their forces used drones in the latest Baidoa conflict and said they would accept drones from any external power. In the north, Puntland and Somaliland formed an alliance in response to the federal government establishing North East State in 2025. These dynamics risk a widening conflict fuelled by the support of foreign powers. 

Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape?

Join experts and policymakers at our Security and Defence Conference for candid analysis of today’s most pressing threats.

Furthermore, these armed conflicts provide an opportunity for terrorist organizations active in Somalia, such as al-Shabaab and ISIS-Somalia. During political crises, security operations against these groups often decline considerably, allowing them to recover and regroup. The deepening armed conflicts between the federal government and opposition groups offers these organizations an opportunity to expand their influence within a multi-layered conflict.   

Given these broader stakes, it is in the interests of all external parties who have relations with the federal government and member states to pursue options for de-escalation between Somali political actors. Considering their intersection with wider regional dynamics in the Horn of Africa and Red Sea, it is also vital that de-escalation efforts are triangulated through regional institutions such as the African Union and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD). 

In the short term, there is a need to facilitate dialogue that can pave the way for an inclusive political agreement on constitutional amendments, electoral issues and interim governance arrangements, with a realistic timetable until elections can be held. Without such an agreement, the risk of a wider protracted conflict will continue to rise.

title: Why the US midterms are a rare foreign policy election
author: LToremark
description:
Why the US midterms are a rare foreign policy election Expert comment LToremark 15 October 2026

US voters are linking economic concerns to the Trump administration’s foreign policy choices. This is bad news for Republicans.

Foreign policy rarely decides US elections. Conventional wisdom is that voters know little, and care less, about international affairs. Instead, they are driven by pocketbook issues, like the price of gas and groceries. As James Carville, an adviser to Bill Clinton, once observed: ‘it’s the economy, stupid’.  But this year, the economy is foreign policy.

There are two important exceptions to the rule that US voters don’t care about foreign policy – and they both apply this year. One, voters care about foreign affairs when an administration’s choices directly affect their daily lives. Two, voters care about what foreign policy choices reveal about a president’s competence as commander-in-chief. 

The upcoming midterms could therefore be a rare foreign policy election – of a kind not seen since 2006 when a backlash to George W. Bush’s handling of the Iraq war handed Republicans a ‘thumping’ defeat. 

With voters now feeling the pain of yet another war in the Middle East and Trump’s tariffs, history could repeat itself. The president seems aware of this risk, sending mixed signals about whether the elections will shape his handling of the war in Iran and striking a deal on diesel exports with Russia to ease the pain at the pump for voters.

But perhaps the bigger question is what Trump does after the midterms, the last major electoral check on his presidency. 

War on the ballot

Give your organization access to trusted geopolitical analysis, policy insight and expert networks to help leaders anticipate risk, navigate uncertainty and make informed decisions.

War has always been the clearest example of when foreign policy directly affects the daily lives of voters.

But this is not always reflected in polls about the importance of individual issues – and this year is no different. Voters cite economic issues as the key drivers of their vote. In a recent survey by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, pluralities of voters across the political spectrum cite inflation and the cost of living as most important to their vote (37 per cent overall). By contrast, only 2 per cent single out the war in Iran as the most important issue, possibly due to the relatively low number of US casualties.

But that does not mean it is not having an impact. Voters are linking the pain in their pocketbooks with the foreign policy choices of this administration. According to a recent survey by the Institute for Global Affairs, 81 per cent of Americans say the war in Iran has increased the cost of living. The Chicago Council survey puts the number even higher, at 86 per cent.

And then there are the trade wars. According to the Chicago Council survey, 81 per cent of respondents say tariffs have been bad for the cost of living. It is unsurprising, therefore, that 75 per cent of Americans say tariffs will be important to their midterm vote, according to a survey by the Cato Institute.

Importantly, these findings cannot be written off as partisanship. Across a whole range of issues, support for Trump’s policies lags well behind his overall approval rating – which continues to hover around a historic low of 37 per cent. This suggests voters are not just instinctively opposing anything the president does but that large numbers of Americans, including many who otherwise support him, do not like his policy choices.

Affordability concerns will still dominate these elections. But large numbers of Americans blame the administration’s foreign policy choices for the perilous state of their household finances. And that’s bad news for Republicans.

From a strong leader to a reckless one

The second exception is when prominent foreign policy missteps tarnish the image of the sitting president in ways that cause voters to take note.

For example, how the Biden administration handled the 2021 US withdrawal from Afghanistan severely damaged perceptions of Joe Biden. His approval rating dropped almost overnight and never recovered.

In 2024, Trump was able to turn this into an advantage on the campaign trail by presenting himself as a strong leader who would stand up against America’s adversaries – and with a commitment to peace.

Today, Trump’s reputation is suffering from both his inability to resolve foreign policy challenges he inherited and the abandonment of his pledge to avoid entangling the US in costly conflicts overseas.

In a CNN/SSRS survey, just 29 per cent of US adults said they approved of Trump’s handling of foreign affairs, down from 42 per cent shortly after he returned to office. Only one in four respondents believed he had a clear strategy for handling Tehran, down from 40 per cent in the immediate aftermath of the outbreak of the war. 

These dynamics also appear to be feeding into broader perceptions of Trump’s leadership. In a YouGov survey fielded at the outset of the war, 56 per cent of respondents said the word ‘reckless’ applied ‘a lot’ to Trump – up five points from a year ago – while the proportion who described him as a ‘strong leader’ dropped four percentage points. 

To what degree will foreign policy shape the results – and how will Trump respond?

Related work

What the US midterms could mean for Trump’s power

Republicans were already likely to fare poorly. The midterms are traditionally seen as a referendum on the performance of the incumbent president, and with Trump’s overall approval ratings at a near-record low, history is not on his side.

Even though foreign policy may not dominate any given race, it is likely to matter at the margins. And in a tight race, that could make all the difference.

In some swing states Republican candidates are distancing themselves from the president’s policies. In Michigan, Senate nominee Mike Rogers has said the war ‘needs to end, and end quickly’, to provide relief for American families. In Iowa, meanwhile, Senate nominee Ashley Hinson similarly said that Iowans ‘shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran’. 

Trump’s diesel deal with Russia indicates some sensitivity to the electoral risks of high gas prices. But achieving this by accommodating Vladimir Putin – rather than an embargo on US diesel exports, for example – has only highlighted another foreign policy weakness: Trump’s inability to end the war in Ukraine.

But will an electoral rebuke result in more foreign policy restraint? Perhaps the most important question is not the degree to which foreign policy will shape the results, but how the president will respond. 

And here, history offers a warning. After his 2006 midterm defeat, President Bush did not change course. Instead, he defied the mandate voters had given by escalating an unpopular war in the Middle East.

President Trump recently pledged not to attack Iran before the midterms, having previously expressed a desire to help his party in the elections. Whether he too will try to end the war through a dramatic escalation once the ballots are counted remains to be seen. 

But he would not be the first president to double down on an unpopular policy once unshackled from electoral constraints. The ‘lame duck’ phase of Trump’s presidency may therefore prove even more disruptive on the international stage.

title: Responding to US sanctions on the International Criminal Court
author: sfarrell.drupal@chathamhouse.org
description:
Responding to US sanctions on the International Criminal Court Expert comment sfarrell.drupa… 15 October 2026

The US decision to extend sanctions has upped the ante in its campaign against the ICC. The Court’s supporters must decide how to respond, perhaps now it is time to put all options on the table.

On 9 October 2026, the US designated the International Criminal Court under Executive Order 14203, extending its existing sanctions package on individual ICC officials to the entity itself as a whole.

The US imposed asset freezes on any property owned by the Court and prohibited all transactions by US individuals or entities involving the ICC.

The US has allowed certain limited exceptions to this general prohibition, to allow for the ongoing detention of some awaiting trial, the payment of pensions, the use of IT software and social media and a 180-day ‘wind down’, allowing certain otherwise prohibited transactions until April 2027.

These sanctions were introduced by the US in what Secretary of State Marco Rubio called an ongoing campaign to ‘dismantle the ICC brick by brick’.

‘For decades, Republicans and Democrats alike rejected the idea that the International Criminal Court had the power to prosecute American citizens, military service members, or political leaders. America never joined the court. We don’t need it. And we don’t want it,’ Rubio said in a statement.

‘We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American service members for their defense, to rein in the court. If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer,’ he added.

The ICC called the sanctions ‘an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do. It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law.’

Those countries that have signed up to the ICC – the ‘State Parties’  – now have to decide how to respond, through diplomacy; support or the ‘nuclear option’.

The impact

An asset freeze essentially prevents making any economic resources available directly or indirectly to the ICC.  They must be observed by all US persons and green card holders, wherever they are in the world, all US companies and any person in the US. 

They also apply to any transactions or data routed through the United States. In reality, this can often limit (at best) and prevent (at worst) nearly all financial transactions of a designated person.

As such, if left unchecked, the US sanctions could severely hamper the day-to-day operations of the ICC.  The General Licence operates to provide a wind down period, but at most provides a stay of execution and the potential for diplomatic efforts to reverse or mitigate the impact.

The Court itself noted that whilst it endeavours to continue functioning as normal, international cooperation is imperative as the Court’s fate also rests in ‘the hands of the States that created it’. 

So far, foreign ministers of the UK and others have issued a Joint Statement affirming their unwavering support for the ICC. The EU has also said that it stands ready ‘to take all necessary measures to ensure the Court continues to operate effectively and fulfils its indispensable mandate’. 

Below are recommendations on how the UK government may best respond to the ICC designation in coalition with other State Parties.

Diplomatic Engagement 

State Parties should open the dialogue as necessary to address the US concerns regarding the authority of the ICC. 

The 180-day Maintenance General Licence, marked as a show of good faith, intends to achieve just that. It provides State Parties the chance for diplomatic engagement.  The ICC’s Assembly of States Parties in December will provide an opportunity to review and align the response of the State Parties to the US.

Practical Support: Preparing for the Worst

In parallel to diplomatic efforts, State Parties can start to consider what practical assistance they can provide in the event that diplomatic efforts are unsuccessful or that companies start de-risking sooner rather than later and start to withdraw services before the expiry of the US General Licences that could impact – as no doubt the US intends – the ongoing investigations and operations of the Court.

As such, whilst the US General Licence might allow for a 180-day ‘wind down’ of the provision of crucial goods and services, companies caught by US sanctions may simply decide to stop working with the Court at any time.

That means the State Parties need a comprehensive plan to support the Court, covering everything from provision of IT to support on banking and payment routes, and everything in between.

Blocking Statute: the Nuclear Option

Some State Parties – in particular the UK and EU Member States – may have the option of turning to the ‘Blocking Statute’.

This has been dubbed the ‘nuclear option’ by Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen. It would essentially prohibit any natural or legal person from complying with US sanctions.

But Blocking Statutes have only been deployed vary rarely in the past, primarily targeting US extra-territorial over-reach where it has imposed sanctions against countries like Cuba and Iran, and required those outside of US jurisdiction to comply with them.

However, even this nuclear option’ is not without its limitations. First, it won’t be available to all State Parties without new primary legislation. Second, even where the legislation is in place, it is not clear that the US measures would fall squarely within the legislation which is designed to protect ‘trading interests’ against extra-territorial measures. An argument could certainly be made, but it could face challenge if ever relied upon.

Third, it only applies to those caught by the relevant jurisdiction. In the UK and EU, for example, the prohibition on complying with the US sanctions would only have to be observed by UK/EU nationals, UK/EU companies or those operating in the UK or EU.

Finally, it essentially puts domestic companies between a rock and a hard place – fail to comply with US sanctions or fail to comply with the UK/EU ‘Blocking Statute’.

State Parties with this potential option have not deployed it despite the US targeting of judges and Court staff; perhaps now the US has upped the ante in its campaign against the Court, it is time for its supporters to put all options on the table.

title: After Trump’s midterm defeat, Russia and China will encounter a cooler US
author: jon.wallace
description:
After Trump’s midterm defeat, Russia and China will encounter a cooler US  Expert comment jon.wallace 5 November 2026

They may seek to exploit the president’s weakness, as domestic opposition to war with Iran hardens.

The comprehensive rebuff that American voters have given to President Donald Trump and Republican candidates in the midterm elections is likely to produce a small but important constraint on how the US behaves abroad. But it will also change how other countries treat it – allies, trading partners and rivals alike. 

Even with the Democrats in control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, the president retains much power over foreign policy – but not all. Congress is now likely to challenge any sustained deployment of forces in the Gulf. And it will reassert its authority over trade and tariffs, even if it does not amend the latter. 

Hear directly from the experts

Get nuanced insights from Chatham House experts on the issues shaping the global policy and geopolitical landscape.

The most immediate change is likely to be on the conflict with Iran. Voters put the cost of living – ‘affordability’ – top of their concerns. Yet, as they went to the polls, gasoline prices at the pump hit a high. Rising costs are largely a result of the continued conflict in and around the Strait of Hormuz, which Americans know Trump initiated alongside Israel and has failed to end. Trump could now indeed ‘lash out’ as some have predicted with more strikes, in an attempt to secure concessions from Tehran. But there is no reason to believe that a military solution will fare any better than before. 

The Republican party has been among the biggest losers from the war. The race for the presidency in 2028 started the moment the midterm results became clear. And GOP candidates are likely to be vehemently against continuing the conflict. Pressure within the US for a resolution will rise even if Benjamin Netanyahu, now Israel’s caretaker prime minister after his own electoral setback, urges a new assault. 

Ukraine

The change in Congress will probably not mean more arms or money for Ukraine. There is deep, rare consensus among both Democrats and Republicans that Europe should now pay its way on its own defence – and that supporting Ukraine is part of that. Trump has won that longstanding argument, they feel, and they have no desire to undermine that victory. 

However, the new Congress does not share Trump’s apparent warmth towards Russian President Vladimir Putin. Traditional hostility or wariness towards Moscow prevails. 

Trump, his son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff might still dangle business deals before the Kremlin, hoping for peace in return. But they will be constrained by a tougher mood and even formal opposition in Congress. No wonder that Putin’s spokesperson said, as the results became clear, that he hoped peace-making efforts would continue.

China

The same congressional wariness may well extend to China. One of the biggest disruptions that Trump could cause in his remaining two years would be to try to strike a deal with Beijing that included explicit acknowledgement of Taiwan as the sovereign territory of China. Trump’s recent decision to pause a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan, to avoid aggravating trade relations with China, could be interpreted by Beijing as support for its views. Congress has, again across the political divide, been much warier of China. It now seems that some tech companies are leaning that way too.

The fate of Trump’s tariffs is unclear. For the moment they will stay, although Congress has been challenging the president’s right to impose them without its consent, through the Supreme Court. 

Politicians of all stripes find tariffs attractive for the revenue they bring. But others will look at the disruption to trade they cause (US car manufacturing was until last year interwoven with Canada’s) and their impact on inflation. That last point is hotly debated among economists given that inflation did not rise as much as expected when the tariffs were first imposed. But politicians in search of securing a lower cost of living may look again at arguments for repealing the tariffs. 

A city on a hill?

Most of all, the elections may change how the world looks at America. They go some way to answering the big questions raised by Trump’s second presidency: Have Americans changed? Are his actions what they really want, given they have voted for him twice? And is US democracy robust and capable of securing peaceful changes of power? To that extent, some will find the results reassuring. 

For US allies in Europe, Japan and South Korea, they may feel more confident in asserting their interests and values – although they will still be nervous of losing US support. Trump’s sudden apparent removal of arms support to Israel in the days before the election shows how whimsical that can be. 

For the US’s enemies and rivals, this result will inject uncertainty into their calculations. But it will also give them reason to probe for weakness, even if that is just by exploiting the repeated changes in policy inherent in the democratic system. Both Russia and China will brace themselves for a cooling of relations. But they will also explore the implications of the US being unable to hold consistently to its key positions for more than a few years. 

Given Trump’s personality and desire for attention, nothing can rule out impetuous and dramatic action, for instance on Iran or Taiwan. But he has lost any aura of being a winner that he retained. Politicians seeking to run in two years’ time will begin to distance themselves from him and try to constrain him from actions that could tarnish their chances. They may hope that he restricts his attention to the memorials in his name he is so keen to create.

title: What will historic US midterm results mean for the future of Democrats and Republicans?
author: LToremark
description:
What will historic US midterm results mean for the future of Democrats and Republicans? Expert comment LToremark 5 November 2026

After a huge win for Democrats, both parties now face a reckoning as they prepare for the 2028 presidential race – and the post-Trump era.

American voters delivered a resounding victory for Democrats in the 2026 midterms, the scale of their win surpassing all expectations. With control of both chambers of Congress – the House of Representatives and the Senate – Democrats will now preside over powerful tools of investigation and oversight, federal spending constraints and the ability to block Trump’s nominees, including for Supreme Court vacancies.

President Trump will remain an enduring presence into the 2028 election cycle, especially on matters of foreign policy. But attention will increasingly move to his potential successors and the parties’ respective visions for the future. How – and whether – Democrats and Republicans use the two years ahead to constrain Trump’s widely unpopular foreign policy and define a clear alternative will determine both their success in claiming the White House and in shaping the global landscape its next resident will inherit.

Related work

Trump is set to redefine the lame duck presidency

Both parties now face a reckoning, with consequential choices ahead on the key issues to prioritise, the ideological purity tests they may seek to impose and the presidential candidate they nominate for 2028.

Democrats face a competitive primary season for the first time in eight years. This offers an opportunity for genuine debate but also risks stoking significant infighting. 

Moderates and conservative Democrats gained significant ground in traditionally Republican bastions. Progressives also notched key victories – from Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan to Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s (AOC) re-election in New York City. But the incoming Democratic caucus will hold very diverse views on issues like the US relationship with Israel, use of military force, defence spending and immigration.

Republicans, meanwhile, face the massive task of revitalizing a party defined by Trump for the last decade – while also managing his likely moves to compel loyalty and cement a MAGA succession plan. The midterm results offer the clearest evidence yet that proximity to Trump will be increasingly untenable. This could open the door for greater independence – and some resistance – among the Republican Congress, particularly on the Iran war and Trump’s entreaties to Vladimir Putin. 

As the Republican party looks ahead to 2028, Trump himself may be one of their biggest obstacles to forging a new platform that retires some of the more unpopular elements of Trump’s legacy – expensive wars, tariff-related economic disruption and allegations of corruption – while retaining winning elements for their base.  

Democrats’ strategy worked. But foreign policy divisions will resurface

The midterms showcased the strength of the Democratic coalition built ahead of the elections, reaching into deep red states and districts like Texas, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and South Carolina. Progressive and moderate wins showed that an inclusive, ‘big tent’ strategy can succeed. Economic populism, labour rights and affordable housing featured across progressive campaigns, while centrist candidates emphasized pragmatic governance, national security and economic competitiveness. Most candidates spoke about lowering the cost of living, ending the Iran war, expanding access to healthcare, and managing AI risks and data centre buildouts. Democrats will now seek to coalesce around an agenda in the House and Senate, stressing party unity.

But the foreign policy fissures that emerged in the midterm primary races have not gone away. After conceding the Congressional losses, President Trump told Fox News he could imagine working with Democrats on immigration – one of the Democratic party’s most persistent fault lines. Reductions in US military spending will also divide the caucus, with many progressives in favour of redirecting overseas funds to domestic revitalization. The US relationship with Israel will be one of the most contested discussions, with a growing number of centrist Democrats pushing for huge foreign assistance cuts for Israel and greater conditionality – if not outright suspension – of arms sales. The rancour in the Michigan Senate race – where Israel featured prominently – offered a preview of fights to come.

The left will continue to be unified in their opposition to Trump. But he will soon be gone. Shaping an affirmative governance agenda in the face of deep intra-party divisions will be the big test into 2028.

A competitive primary season that fosters open debate among the Democratic presidential candidates will expose these divisions. But the anointing of Biden/Harris in 2024 denied the party the chance to grapple with genuine differences and work to shape an inclusive, representative platform. This process will be painful but necessary. The final presidential nominee among the dozen plus anticipated to enter the field – from Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff to New York’s AOC – will offer the clearest signal of the party’s direction of travel.

Republicans must forge a post-Trump future

The Republican party has suffered one of its worst defeats in years, if not decades. It now turns to the sobering reality of navigating both the future of the party and the end of the Trump era. Their vision for the future will need to resonate not only with MAGA voters, but also centrist Republicans and Independents whose absence in the midterms cost the party dearly. Although candidates’ messaging around illegal immigration and violent crime align with Republican voter concerns, they failed to break through.

Trump’s record disapproval ratings was a further drag on Republican and Independent turnout. Loyalty tests meant candidates had to run on Trump’s record, a tricky proposition as voters connected the war in Iran with affordability. Republicans were also saddled with several troubled, scandal-marred candidates like Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton and Ohio House incumbent Max Miller. Trump himself is unlikely to do much soul searching, exclaiming on Truth Social ‘I wasn’t on the ballot, and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!’.  But the Republican party will be forced to reckon with these results as they forge their post-Trump future.

Trump’s relationship with the party will be biggest fissure on the right. As 2028 approaches, Republican candidates may see greater peril in sticking with Trump than beginning to distance themselves. Republicans may also struggle to hold the caucus together and avoid backstabbing and defections, particularly if Democrats’ investigations succeed in unseating senior officials.

On substance, Republicans may be increasingly divided on whether to change course on some of Trump’s unpopular foreign policy moves. Some Republican officials have publicly criticized Trump on Greenland and the Iran war, but more may see political value in critiquing wider swaths of his foreign policy – beginning with Trump’s interest in a trade deal with China or an accommodation with Putin. This will be particularly challenging for the anticipated Republican nominees, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who will remain closely associated with Trump’s unpopular policies. Vance has publicly blamed the Iran war for the midterms defeat and also cited Republican voters’ desire for a different relationship with Israel, likely a factor in Trump’s surprise election day announcement that he would suspend $4 billion in annual assistance to Israel.

Trump will soon be departing after a decade as darling of the right and foil for the left. This leaves both parties facing difficult choices. Whether Democrats can unite around a broad coalition or Republicans can wrest their political fate from Trump remains to be seen. Two years from now, a new president may still inherit many of problems created or exacerbated by Trump, including a global tariff regime, a protracted war in Iran and fractured alliances. The central challenge for both Republicans and Democrats will be not simply to reconstitute what has been broken, drawing on what worked in the past. Each will need a new vision.

title: Easy money does not win elections
author: Yao Chen, Felix Ward, Florian van Genderen
description: Politicians have long pressed central banks for lower interest rates in the belief that easy money wins elections. This column tests that premise using 385 parliamentary and presidential elections in 18 countries between 1900 and 2020. It finds no evidence that easy money helps incumbents. title: Lula wins Brazil’s presidential election; Trump says vote looks ‘rigged’: Early analysis from Chatham House experts
author: jon.wallace
description:
Lula wins Brazil’s presidential election; Trump says vote looks ‘rigged’: Early analysis from Chatham House experts Expert comment jon.wallace 25 October 2026

What does Lula’s unexpected victory mean for Brazil’s democracy and economy? How will foreign policy develop on the US and China? And what does this mean for the Bolsonaro family and Brazil? Chatham House experts provide insights.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, commonly known as Lula, has been re-elected president of Brazil for a fourth term. Lula secured 51.79 per cent of the vote against Bolsonaro’s 48.21 per cent. 

The victory was a surprise: Lula’s opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, led in the first round of the election held on 4 October. The result was announced after an unusual decision on Sunday by the country’s Supreme Court, which allowed polling centres to remain open longer than planned. 

Lula said of his victory:

‘This, my fourth term, will be the best of any president in the history of this country’.

Defeated candidate Bolsonaro initially refused to accept the result, saying: 

‘It is impossible to recognize the election results, given the circumstances under which things unfolded.’

A spokesman for Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party later said they accepted the result, but still had concerns about the election process. On Monday President Donald Trump said the election looked ‘rigged’.

Below, Chatham House experts provide analysis of the meaning of the result for Brazilians, the region and the world.

Eduardo Vasconcelos on Brazil’s Supreme Court
Dr Christopher Sabatini on what next for US relations?
Dr Bruno Binetti on Brazil’s China policy
Vanessa Rubio Marquez on the left and right in Latin America
Luis Miguel Castilla Rubio on Lula’s policies and Brazil’s economy

Lula’s victory and reform of the Supreme Court

Eduardo Vasconcelos, Academy Fellow, Latin America Programme

About 35,000 Brazilians voted after polls were due to close at 5PM on Sunday, most in the first five minutes as queues cleared. Only some 5,300 votes came after 5.05PM, when the Supreme Court’s two-hour extension could have made a difference. 

Those few thousand votes may not have decided the election – Lula won by 4.4 million votes – but the extension of voting cost Brazil, as it gave Flávio Bolsonaro his pretext to question the result. Bolsonaro’s party has conceded defeat and Bolsonaro has refrained from disputing Lula’s victory. But he has still cast doubt on the process, saying ‘It was not me who lost, it was the system which won’.

On polling day, Lula’s campaign complained that buses had stopped running in several cities; Flávio’s team also asked for extra time in towns hit by heavy rain. The Superior Electoral Court was still weighing both requests when Lula’s campaign went to the Supreme Court. A single justice, Cristiano Zanin, extended voting nationwide minutes after polls had closed. Closed machines could not be reopened. In the same neighbourhood, one voter might still cast a ballot while another was turned away.

Zanin’s decision was the final act of a campaign season in which judges were called upon more than ever to set the terms of competition. By 21 October the electoral court had received 804 legal challenges over the presidential race, against 325 at the same point in 2022. 

This has come at a time when the Supreme Court’s reputation is badly tarnished, after it failed to decide whether to investigate one of its own justices. Three in four Brazilians say its members have too much power. A record 48 per cent distrust it.

Brazil’s courts used extraordinary powers to protect the 2022 election from an authoritarian threat. After this election, the country now faces a new task. It must constrain the Court’s powers within ordinary limits, so that no single judge can change the rules on election day again.

Three reforms would help improve the Court’s reputation. Decisions that alter electoral rules or suspend laws passed by Congress should require the full Court. Justices should serve fixed terms. And misconduct cases against justices should be decided within set deadlines. Majorities of both Lula’s and Flávio’s voters back full-court decisions and fixed terms. 

Lula may fill four seats on the Court by 2030. Each will need 41 Senate votes, giving senators leverage to demand reform. They must put aside squabbling to cohere behind voters’ wishes and compel reform of the system. Without it, trust in Brazil’s institutions may suffer even more.

What next for US relations? 

Christopher Sabatini, Director of Chatham House’s Latin America Programme

While President Donald Trump claimed Brazil’s second round presidential election looked ‘rigged’ on Monday, other heads of state rushed to recognize President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s unexpected second-round presidential victory over conservative Flávio Bolsonaro.  

French President Emmanuel Macron, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney all publicly congratulated Lula on his victory. Even Brazil’s more conservative neighbours joined the chorus, including Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa, Chilean President José Antonio Kast, and Paraguayan President Santiago Peña.  

The White House’s response is not surprising. It had been counting on the election of Bolsonaro to complete its bingo card of right-wing presidents in the Western Hemisphere, following a period of sustained electoral success for right-wing candidates stretching from Honduras to Argentina. But Latin American regional solidarity and respect for democratic institutions and the popular will trumped ideology and alignment with the US. 

Adding Latin America’s largest democracy and economy would have represented a major victory for the self-proclaimed ‘Donroe Doctrine’. Instead, public support for Lula’s re-election may demonstrate that the bloc of Trump-aligned and Trump-adjacent presidents may not be as strong and ideological as many thought. (Only Argentine President Javier Milei has withheld congratulations for Lula.)

After initially calling for an annulment, members of the defeated candidate’s team said the party accepted the results but questioned the conditions of the election process. Unlike his father, Jair, did in 2022 when he lost to Lula, Flávio seems to be walking back an outright rejection of the election, while still undermining public confidence in the election results. 

Their questions over how the situation unfolded hinges on a Supreme Court justice who supported Lula’s Workers’ Party request to extend voting by two hours on Sunday. That request was made originally by both parties to Brazil’s electoral court – in order to accommodate voters who struggled to make it to the booths due to heavy rains, and others allegedly affected by limited public transportation. But the decision to kick the request up to the Supreme Court after the electoral court failed to respond casts a pall over the results – and further threatens the reputation of a Supreme Court already under suspicion for being politicized.

Brazil’s modern, transparent voting system will be able to demonstrate the results – for those who want to believe them. But for core Bolsonaro supporters, trusting the results may be difficult. Flávio’s father also claimed unproven fraud in 2022. And father and son have baked distrust of the judicial and electoral system into their political DNA, polarizing politics and society in Brazil.  

In the end, how far Flávio’s team decides to take its claims of fraud may depend on the White House and the US State Department. Both had a lot riding on a Bolsonaro victory. For Trump it would have been the crowning achievement for his support in the region, during this heavy year of presidential elections across the hemisphere.  

For others the issue is more ideological and personal. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, like many Cuban-Americans, saw Lula’s Workers’ Party as complicit in upholding the communist regimes in Cuba and Nicaragua. Creating a ring of conservative, anti-communist governments across the hemisphere to stand with the US against those regimes has long been a dream of Republican administrations and Cuban-Americans in Florida. Their perspective will likely also help decide whether and when the Trump administration accepts a Lula victory.

With conservative majorities in both houses of Congress, Lula will have a difficult time attempting to tackle the economic and fiscal reforms necessary to keep the government solvent and address its looming sovereign debt. But the biggest loser in the election is social trust. The country’s voters are now almost evenly split between Bolsonaro and Lula (only 3.6 per cent separated the two leaders). And popular confidence in the Supreme Court may decline even more.

Will Lula change Brazil’s approach to China?

Bruno Binetti, Associate Fellow, Latin America Programme

Lula’s re-election, following a campaign in which he declared that Brazil was ‘nobody’s backyard’ and denounced foreign interference, will be welcomed in Beijing. 

China retains a close partner in Latin America’s largest economy, at a time when most countries in the region have moved closer to the Trump administration. Lula shares China’s commitment to a multipolar international order with a stronger role for the Global South. That includes efforts within BRICS to reduce reliance on the US dollar in international trade, reform global financial institutions and expand climate finance for developing countries.

This partnership is underpinned by strong economic ties – ties so important they would have endured a Bolsonaro victory. China has been Brazil’s largest trading partner since 2009, driven by Brazilian exports of soybeans, iron ore and crude oil. In 2025, Brazilian exports to China reached $100 billion, compared with $38 billion to the US. This makes continued engagement with Beijing a priority for the powerful agribusiness sector, which is well represented in Congress and traditionally aligned with Bolsonaro and the political right.

Brazil was also the world’s largest recipient of Chinese investment in 2025, with Chinese firms expanding their presence in electricity infrastructure, manufacturing and mining. In the automotive sector, BYD and Great Wall Motor have established electric vehicle production facilities in Brazil, and Lula is pushing Chinese manufacturers to use more local suppliers and create jobs.

Brazil-China relations are likely to deepen during Lula’s fourth term, especially if the Trump administration continues to impose tariffs and other trade restrictions on Brazil. 

Yet Lula is the ultimate pragmatist. He has always sought to maintain good relations with competing powers. Brazil and the US are already discussing a potential trade agreement that could include cooperation on critical minerals, a top priority for Washington as it tries to reduce dependence on China. 

With the world’s second-largest rare-earth reserves, Lula is open to investment from both China and the US, provided it helps Brazil develop its own processing industries and move up the value chain,

What does this result mean for the left and right in Latin America?

Vanessa Rubio Marquez, Associate Fellow, Latin America Programme

With Lula’s clear victory in the presidential run-off on 25 October, the two largest Latin American economies, Brazil and Mexico, will be perceived as the remaining guardians of the left, in a region that has largely flipped to the right of the political spectrum in recent years. However, the more relevant question is whether being left or right in the Western Hemisphere – and the world – still means what it once did.

Traditionally, the distinction between left and right was relatively clear. The left favoured a stronger role for the state in reducing inequality and redistributing wealth. The right, by contrast, placed greater emphasis on individual responsibility, private enterprise and preserving existing economic and social structures, accepting inequalities as a natural feature of society.

Today, these boundaries are being blurred. For instance, under Jair Bolsonaro, Brazil increased minimum monthly welfare transfers by 50 per cent (R$400 to R$600), reaching over 20 million families ahead of the 2022 election. And the reduction of the working week from 44 to 40 hours also took place under his mandate. Similar measures to protect specific sectors in society were implemented in Ecuador, where right-wing Daniel Noboa introduced financial assistance for vulnerable entrepreneurs. 

However, the left -wing Mexican government of Andrés Manuel López Obrador limited pandemic spending and direct budget support to 0.7 per cent of GDP, compared with over 3 per cent across G20 emerging economies. And Chile’s left-wing president, Gabriel Boric, oversaw a 23.1 per cent real reduction in government spending in 2022.

Ever more, the extremes of left and right converge in pragmatic, immediate and populist policies. The more important divide is how governments exercise power, respect democratic institutions and protect individual freedoms while they deliver for the people. 

A very interesting case of a tension between democracy and tangible results in matters that people prioritise is seen in El Salvador. President Nayib Bukele’s crackdown on gangs has brought major security gains, but at a cost to civil liberties. Emergency powers have been extended 55 times since 2022, with over 93,000 arrests and restrictions on due process.

Being the ‘remaining two of the left’ matters less than how the countries that jointly produce more than 88 per cent of Latin America’s GDP are governed. 

Lula’s victory reminds us of a broader, more concerning regional trend: the defining divide is increasingly between governments that preserve democratic institutions and individual freedoms and those willing to weaken them for ideological, political and electoral reasons.

Can Brazil afford Lula’s promised spending?

Luis Miguel Castilla, Associate Fellow, Latin America Programme 

Lula returns for a fourth term to a Congress where the right and the Centrão hold the larger share of seats, and where the Centrão is expected to hold over 170. The agenda he promised, which includes a university stipend, a new round of household debt relief and a larger housing programme, will be hard to achieve: the president must negotiate with a majority whose incentives lie in protecting its own share of the budget.

Fiscal rigidities leave little room for any of Lula’s agenda. Barely 10 per cent of the budget is discretionary. Congress will resist new taxes. That will leave cutting expenditure. But that will also not be easy, when legislators will defend parliamentary amendments and indexed mandatory items. 

Interest payments neared 7.7 per cent of GDP in 2024 and 8.05 per cent in 2025, claiming resources that might otherwise have been spent on Lula’s social agenda. On the authorities’ definition, Brazil’s gross debt will reach 86.6 per cent of GDP this year and 94.1 per cent by 2030. By the IMF’s broader measure it already exceeds 97 per cent. Moving the central government primary balance from a deficit of 0.2 per cent of GDP in 2026 to a surplus of 0.1 per cent in 2027 – as Lula has projected – will be unlikely without an understanding with the Centrão on those amendments and on indexation.

Brazil’s credit ratings are in the BB range, below investment grade, reflecting this picture. Agencies will judge the new government by its early decisions on the spending rule and the amendments: a rigid budget and heavy interest costs will limit any improvement in risk perception. A downgrade would raise borrowing costs and enlarge the interest bill, further shrinking the space for social programmes.

Growth would offer a route that will not depend on legislators’ preferences. Yet forecasts of about 2 per cent this year, slowing in 2027, fall short of what the debt requires when real interest rates are near 9.5 per cent. Higher potential growth depends on implementing VAT reform and raising productivity. Both take years to materialize.

Lula will argue that voters have endorsed his expansionary course, and that well-targeted social programmes can support growth. A mandate, however, leaves the interest bill and the preferences of Congress unchanged. 

A workable course will need to pair a credible spending rule with a medium-term debt anchor, with transparent rules on amendments that give the Centrão predictable influence in return for restraint. Room for Lula’s social agenda will then lie in the quality of spending and in faster growth, within the limits that Congress and debt impose.

title: Burnham’s first budget should take a global approach to deliver for the UK
author: thilton.drupal
description:
Burnham’s first budget should take a global approach to deliver for the UK Expert comment thilton.drupal 26 October 2026

The cost of living, growth and jobs are all impacted by global geoeconomics. To pass the ‘Makerfield Test’ and deliver for ordinary people, the budget should recognize this and build resilience to external shocks.

This week’s budget, the first of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government, will aim to reduce the cost of living and deliver growth and jobs. It faces a major challenge: much of what impacts both these objectives is set abroad.

I have previously argued for an international form of Burnham’s ‘Manchesterism.’ This ‘International Manchesterism’ should recognize that global forces are inseparable from local outcomes. Therefore, domestic priorities will be achieved only if the government recognizes and puts to use the two-way link between the domestic and the international. 

Its success can be measured by applying the ‘Makerfield Test’ (a reference to Burnham’s constituency in northern England) to foreign policy, which provides a framework for assessing whether the government’s international choices tangibly improve life in Britain’s communities. The test has several key pillars including economic security, energy resilience and rebalancing investment towards underserved regions. 

The budget is where those pillars meet the public finances. Burnham has promised better public services and lower bills. But these rest on global gas markets, food and fertiliser supply chains, and investor confidence. 

In this budget, Chancellor John Healey should therefore treat geoeconomics not just as context, but as a key fiscal variable. The budget cannot deliver on the cost of living, growth or jobs through domestic tax and spend alone. 

Cost of living: energy and food

Energy resilience is central to the Makerfield Test, and household energy is where the exposure is most visible. Currently, electricity prices in the UK are set mainly by gas prices, leaving the UK more vulnerable to global price spikes than many comparable countries.

Ofgem, the UK energy regulator, lifted the price cap by about £60 a year to £1,723 in October as the Iran war drove up wholesale gas. Analysts now forecast a further 16 per cent rise in energy bills from January. 

The prime minister wants to break the link between energy bills and international gas prices. That will take years, which is why the budget must start the work now. 

Food has received far less attention. The Food and Drink Federation expects food inflation to pass 6 per cent by mid-2027. It cites energy costs driven by the conflict in the Middle East, drought and El Niño. Fertiliser, which is made using gas, adds to this pressure. 

Food and energy also shape how households perceive inflation, foods prices especially, as Bank of England research shows. A spike in either can keep interest rates higher for longer.

Growth and jobs: capital and barriers

Growth needs investment, and long-overlooked British regions in particular could benefit from international investment. 

But this depends on the cost of borrowing. A global bond sell-off pushed the 30-year gilt yield briefly above 6 per cent this month and ate into the chancellor’s fiscal headroom, which may yet shrink further. This raises borrowing costs and squeezes the room for the public investment on which growth plans rely.

The budget is also being set out in a period of global economic insecurity. Britain’s largest partners are raising economic barriers and deploying economic leverage. The US has embraced tariffs. The EU is strengthening its economic and trade defence mechanisms. China has leveraged its dominance of rare earths while also pushing its exports aggressively. 

Each of these moves changes the terms on which UK firms invest, trade and hire. Achieving economic security, the Makerfield Test’s first pillar, now requires factoring in these partners’ choices as well as market volatility. This applies to the budget too.

Recognizing the link

The Treasury tends to treat all this as background to the forecast. Traditionally, the Office for Budget Responsibility models the sensitivities, the numbers are adjusted, and policy carries on. 

That worked when global markets were calm, and cooperation with traditional allies could be taken for granted. Neither holds now. 

The Iran war has shown how global developments rapidly impact UK households and the national debt via inflation and interest rates. Costlier energy and food push up inflation, inflation pushes up rates, and higher rates raise the cost of capital that growth depends on. 

The budget therefore needs to put geoeconomics at its centre. It must build resilience against shocks Britain cannot prevent while also signalling a path to growth that investors can price. 

Five recommendations for the budget

This week’s budget should seek to measure, reduce, share and capitalize on Britain’s international exposure. Five measures will help achieve this.

1. Set targets to reduce exposure

The budget should measure Britain’s international exposure and set targets to reduce it. It should publish a short statement alongside the budget that details how finances and household budgets are sensitive to global borrowing costs, gas prices and food import prices. 

This should include measurable targets to bring that sensitivity down over this parliament. This becomes the yardstick against which the other measures outlined here are judged.

2. Cut energy bills by reducing gas dependence

The budget should take three measures to cut household energy bills by reducing gas dependence. 

Want to hear more on the path to a secure energy transition?

Join us at our climate and energy summit, where policymakers and industry leaders tackle the toughest questions on climate and energy security.

It should move the remaining quarter of the Renewables Obligation’s cost to general taxation and also review other policy costs still levied on electricity bills, making electricity cheaper relative to gas.

It should also bring forward spending under the £15 billion Warm Homes Plan, prioritizing insulation in the least efficient homes. 

And it should secure gas storage. By one estimate, Britain holds around 12 days of gas storage, compared with 89 in Germany. Its largest site, Rough, could close next spring without a deal. This should be prevented. 

Crucially, all of this should be classed as investment that reduces risk, protected within the capital budget (rather than treated as short-term relief), and co-financed through the National Wealth Fund wherever possible. 

3. Protect food supply against the next fertiliser shock

Britain’s last large ammonia plant, at Billingham, closed in 2023 because UK gas prices made it uncompetitive. Fertiliser is now made from imported ammonia sourced at global prices. 

The budget should fund a strategic fertiliser reserve large enough to see farmers through a season of disruption. It should also use the National Wealth Fund to support low-carbon ammonia production linked to the UK’s hydrogen projects. 

4. Build economic security

The budget should scale up the £50 million critical minerals fund announced last year to fund a stockpile of minerals most exposed to supply chain disruption of export controls. 

This could be done via expanding UK Export Finance guarantees to diversify minerals supply for British manufacturers across more countries. And it should set UK carbon border levy to protect British industry while exempting partners that do price carbon comparably, starting with the EU.  

5. Treat UK credibility as an asset

Multi-year spending plans are already standard for government departments, but there is a gap in specific commitments that generates uncertainty for investors. Defence is the clearest case. 

The chancellor has deferred a path to higher defence spending to next year’s spending review. Setting out that trajectory, and how it will be funded, will remove a major source of uncertainty. 

Beyond the budget

The budget cannot achieve these objectives alone. Some of the most important and complementary steps fall to diplomacy in the following months. 

Related work

Burnham should use a ‘Makerfield Test’ to ground UK foreign policy in real places

The UK-EU summit on 20 November is a chance to secure the linking of emissions trading systems, strengthening British exporters and putting the focus on energy and food supply. 

Canada’s proposed Defence, Security and Resilience Bank offers a way to share defence costs. 

And the UK’s upcoming G20 presidency offers the ideal platform to strengthen shared resilience on energy markets, food and fertiliser security, and sovereign debt.

None of this is a distraction from the cost of living or from growth. It is how both are delivered. A budget that recognizes and reduces the UK’s exposure to global forces is sound economics and good politics. This way, the Treasury can pass the Makerfield Test and deliver for British people.

title: Water has emerged as a key issue for Arizona voters ahead of US midterms – governments should take note
author: LToremark
description:
Water has emerged as a key issue for Arizona voters ahead of US midterms – governments should take note Expert comment LToremark 12 October 2026

The case of Arizona shows that governments must stop treating water as merely an environmental issue.

US President Donald Trump may dismiss the threat posed by climate change, but its consequences are becoming harder for US voters to ignore. Take Arizona, for example, where water has emerged as an unusually prominent issue ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. Recent polling found that long-term water supplies was the top concern for Arizona voters, after federal cuts to the state’s water supply from the drought-stricken Colorado River. Water has consequently become a prominent issue in Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs’ re-election campaign, with opponents accusing her of mismanaging Arizona’s water supply in an effort to undermine her bid for a second term.

Water is no longer just an environmental issue 

Arizona is an extreme example, but the underlying dynamic is much broader.
Water is fundamental not only to drinking and sanitation, but to almost every aspect of an economy. In Arizona, it underpins agriculture and urban development, while also supporting industries and amenities that can seem particularly incongruous in a desert environment, such as golf courses. Now a new source of demand is emerging: data centres, driven by the rapid growth of cloud computing and artificial intelligence. The Phoenix metropolitan area ranks second in North America for proposed data-centre development, raising questions about the impact of these energy- and water-intensive facilities on already stretched water supply – an emerging big issue in the midterms. 

Related work

AI water usage requires governments to rethink their approach to water

Arizona’s water predicament is being intensified by a changing climate. Already one of the hottest and driest states in the US, Arizona is experiencing rising temperatures that increase evaporation and water demand, while intensifying drought. This is also putting further pressure on the Colorado River, which supplies more than a third of Arizona’s population, while groundwater reserves are being depleted in parts of the state. 

But climate change is only part of the story. Water crises are rarely caused by climate alone. Decades of groundwater over-abstraction, inefficient agricultural practices, pollution, poorly maintained infrastructure and allocations based on historical assumptions can turn a drought into a systemic crisis.

And this is not only an American problem. Cape Town’s 2018 ‘Day Zero’ crisis demonstrated how quickly drought, population growth and rising demand can turn water scarcity into a political emergency. Tehran offers another warning, where drought and declining rainfall have combined with groundwater depletion, and decades of water-management decisions to produce a systemic crisis. European cities like Barcelona, Madrid, Athens, Rome and even London have all faced emergency water restrictions in recent years as drought intensifies.

Companies are paying attention too. The World Economic Forum’s global risk assessments have repeatedly identified water supply shortages among the risks facing economies and businesses. Water shortages can disrupt agricultural supply chains, manufacturing, electricity generation, construction, real estate and technology infrastructure.

Water security is increasingly also about economic and political security.

When water crosses borders, scarcity becomes political

The political challenge becomes even harder when water crosses administrative boundaries.

Arizona’s position within the Colorado River system is governed by a complex web of agreements and legal arrangements, some dating back more than a century. The 1968 legislation authorizing the Central Arizona Project, for example, gave its Colorado River deliveries junior priority, meaning Arizona would face reductions before California in specified shortage circumstances.

As the river comes under increasing pressure, these historical arrangements have become politically consequential. The latest federal proposals for managing the Colorado River envisage substantial reductions in water deliveries to the three lower-basin states – Arizona, California and Nevada – with Arizona facing particularly significant cuts: 27 per cent this year and reductions could nearly double after 2028 if the drought worsens.

The underlying problem is therefore not simply that there is less water. It is that agreements and institutions designed for a different hydrological reality are being used to distribute a resource whose availability is becoming more uncertain.

Related work

The Climate Briefing: Contested waters in international politics

The same dynamic exists internationally. For example, Ethiopia’s plans to develop three new hydropower projects on the Blue Nile have reignited tensions with Egypt, which remains concerned about how upstream water is stored and managed, particularly during drought. The long-running dispute over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam illustrates how greater hydrological variability and more frequent drought can put existing water-sharing arrangements under growing strain.

Water can therefore become a geopolitical issue even when that is not the intention. When a river or reservoir crosses political boundaries, a reduction in supply also becomes a question of who gets less.

Policymakers must move beyond crisis management 

Arizona offers a particularly vivid warning, not only to the US government but to governments around the world, because water has become a political issue before it has run out. 

The first step is to stop treating water primarily as an environmental issue. It is increasingly central to decisions on infrastructure, industry, agriculture, housing and public health, and, where water crosses borders, to foreign and security policy.

Water availability needs to be considered much earlier in decisions about where and how economies grow. If a region is chronically water-stressed, governments – as well as regional, state and local authorities – should ask whether new housing, agriculture or industrial development can be supported by available water supplies over the long term.

Technology will have an important role. Wastewater recycling, leakage reduction, precision irrigation, improved groundwater monitoring, more efficient cooling systems and, in some coastal locations, desalination can help expand the options available.

But technology alone cannot change the realities of water availability. The harder question is therefore what societies choose to build – and where.

This is also where nature-based solutions come in. Restoring wetlands can improve water storage, filter pollutants and reduce flood risk. Protecting watersheds can support groundwater recharge and improve downstream water quality. Restoring degraded soils and changing agricultural practices can improve water retention and reduce irrigation requirements.

These measures can deliver several benefits simultaneously – water security, biodiversity, flood protection, carbon storage and resilience to extreme heat – often at lower cost than purely engineered alternatives.

Finally, governments need to integrate water, land use, energy, agriculture and economic planning, both domestically and with neighbouring countries that share water sources, using realistic projections of future water availability rather than historical averages. Water-sharing arrangements should also be revisited as conditions change, before scarcity turns technical disagreements into political crises.

The emergence of water as a political issue in Arizona is striking in a political environment dominated by concerns over the cost of living, immigration and the Iran war. The fact that it has become a leading concern among voters in one of America’s fastest-growing states shows that water security is crossing an important threshold: from an environmental concern that governments can defer, to a question about what kind of future is physically possible.

title: Will the US and Iran return to war?
author: jon.wallace
description:
Will the US and Iran return to war?  Expert comment jon.wallace 9 November 2026

That is not only President Trump’s decision. Iran may also reignite the conflict, in an attempt to break the US blockade.

In recent weeks there has been considerable speculation that the US would carry out new attacks on Iran once the US midterm elections were concluded. But with the vote complete, Washington’s next move remains unclear. 

In a recent 60 minutes interview US President Donald Trump said he did not see ‘any reason’ to escalate the war. It is possible that the president chooses not to resume military operations against Iran and settles for continuing the current policy of economic strangulation. But even in that case, a return to armed conflict cannot be ruled out. Tehran is unlikely to absorb US pressure quietly while its economy further deteriorates. This is the irony of the US naval blockade of Iran. There’s evidence to suggest it has effectively hurt the regime’s finances. Iran loaded no oil onto tankers in September according to some analyses. 

But the blockade is unlikely to succeed in achieving the strategic objective of forcing the regime to make significant concessions at the bargaining table. Instead, it might push Tehran to lash out, which would take all parties back to square one in this conflict.

Stalemate

The blockade of Iranian oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz has evolved over the past few months. Washington launched the operation back in April; eased it after agreeing to the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Iran in June (which allowed for the reopening of the Strait); then reinstated it on 14 July as the deal unravelled.

Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape?

Join experts and policymakers at our Security and Defence Conference for candid analysis of today’s most pressing threats.

Iran wants the blockade lifted and its conditions met before it reopens and stops its attacks in the Strait. Washington wants concessions on Iran’s nuclear programme before resuming any talks on maritime security.

It’s a stalemate. But it may not last long. The deep distrust between the two sides will make Iran doubt that US concessions will be durable enough to bring it lasting economic relief. Some in the regime will believe it is better for Iran to fight on its own terms than collapse from within as the economy is throttled. 

It will not necessarily require a new US military strike on its territory for Iran to lash out at its neighbours. In 2019, Iran responded to Trump’s economic ‘maximum pressure’ tactics with a series of attacks. In May and June of that year, it struck tankers near Fujairah and in the Gulf of Oman and shot down a US surveillance drone. 

Then on 14 September, drones and missiles hit Saudi Aramco’s Abqaiq processing facility and the Khurais oil field. The Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen claimed responsibility, but the US and Saudi blamed Iran. The message from Tehran was clear: We will respond to extreme economic pressure by attacking Gulf energy infrastructure. 

Defending a founding narrative

There are two main reasons why Iran responded this way to economic pressure before – and why it may do so again. 

The first is ideological. Iran isn’t just defending its shipping lanes and oil exports in this war. It is protecting its founding narrative of sacrifice and endurance. This is what Washington still doesn’t seem to get.

Since its founding, the Islamic Republic has staked its reputation on not just resisting outside pressure but also defying it. Sanctions, isolation, and military threats won’t coerce or bring down the regime: that’s the message Tehran keeps telling its constituencies and adversaries. The war with Iraq of 1980 to 1988 provides the clearest illustration of the regime’s commitment to that principle. Iran fought the war almost on its own, against an adversary backed by the US and Gulf states, and it survived. A difficult year or two as a result of a blockade is hardly comparable to what the regime endured at that time. 

The second reason is practical: Iranian defiance, unlike during the Iraq war, is now aided by outsiders. The biggest source of support is China, through its purchasing of Iranian oil. No wonder US officials have reportedly urged Beijing to play a more constructive role in ending the conflict. They understand that without China, the regime’s staying power will drastically diminish.

Tehran also knows that the Gulf states want the blockade to end. The status quo is causing them tremendous economic pain. The Iranian leadership is betting that if it holds out long enough, those with the most to lose from this economic crisis – Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, and Kuwait – will press Washington harder to find an exit. 

There are limits to Iranian resilience, of course. In 1988, after Operation Praying Mantis (a one-off US strike against Iranian naval resources ordered by President Ronald Reagan) and months of mounting losses, Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini accepted a ceasefire with Iraq. He famously likened it to drinking poison. Yet it showed that when its survival was at stake, Iran could concede (if not surrender).

But the blockade is not the same situation at all. In 1988, there was no way Iran could have won the war. Continuing would have probably led to military collapse. 

Today Iran believes it has the upper hand. Listen to statements by Iranian officials, and it is clear they believe they have already won this contest. That’s partly true. The Iranian regime will, most likely, survive this conflict and possibly avert a new major US attack, which it would define as victory. 

But it still has to address the blockade. If history is any guide, Iran will at some point resort to violence to try to force Washington to reconsider. That, in turn, is unlikely to succeed: the US has its pride, too, and its interests. US officials are convinced that the blockade is working, so giving it up won’t be easy. If anything, Washington is doubling down by giving US Central Command the green light to establish a new task force meant to ‘prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials.’

There’s only one way out of this stalemate: phased diplomacy, which the two sides are apparently considering. The basic sequencing is clear: In the first phase, Washington would need to partially lift the blockade in exchange for Iran reopening the Strait and ceasing all attacks against shipping. In the second, nuclear talks could take place, including the gradual lifting of sanctions and the release of frozen Iranian funds.

The two sides are keen to end the conflict. But they appear equally determined to avoid any perceived humiliation and Israel remains an unpredictable factor. Even now, it is not clear that sense will prevail.
