title: Sánchez’s gamble: This ‘all-in’ election will have international impact
author: jon.wallace
description:
Sánchez’s gamble: This ‘all-in’ election will have international impact Expert comment jon.wallace 5 October 2026

Announcing the election, Sánchez set himself in opposition to President Trump and Javier Milei as well as Spain’s populist right. Much will depend on the prime minister’s ability to rally a fragmented left.

The decision by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to call a snap election is a risky move, but he will have felt he had little choice. His decision fires the starting gun on a year of vital and polarized elections across Europe.

The announcement is not entirely unexpected. Spain was required to hold an election by August 2027 anyway. And Sánchez’s multiparty coalition has looked fragile since it formed in July 2023: it has not passed a full budget since. 

In January, the government approved a decree that regularized the status of 500,000 undocumented migrants and asylum seekers – a move unusual among EU countries generally committed to tightening migration restrictions. In July, the Spanish enclave of Ceuta was overwhelmed by a surge of tens of thousands of migrants, leading to criticism of government policy from within Spain and abroad, including US President Donald Trump. 

This month, a new issue has arisen, as protests grow over housing affordability. The protests prompted the government to introduce emergency legislation, only to see the bill rejected by Spain’s Parliament late last week. This gave Sánchez his opening to call a general election, arguing that ‘to do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people’. 

What are Sánchez’s chances?

Sánchez is a proven survivor and faced similar difficulties in 2023. But calling an election now is a gamble. The summer’s crises have given his political opponents plenty to work with, and trouble assails the prime minister and his party, the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE), from every side. 

The opposition on the right will use the January decree and images of the Ceuta crisis to rally their vote and criticize the government’s competence. The left will point out the housing crisis has deteriorated under Sánchez. Then there are the corruption scandals that plague the prime minister. Some of his closest political allies are embroiled in the Koldo case – an investigation into corruption in health procurement contracts during the COVID-19 pandemic. In a separate case, the prime minister’s own wife has been charged with embezzlement and corruption.

To survive, Sánchez will use the same playbook that worked for him in 2023, where he characterized the contest as a choice between ‘Sanchismo’ (his brand of social democrat politics) or a ‘backward-looking’ far right. 

Related work

The Ceuta border crisis heaps pressure on Spain’s Sánchez government – and European unity

His hope will be that opposition to the PP right wing opposition party – and far right Vox party in particular – will mobilize left wing voters in a highly polarized contest. Vox leader Santiago Abascal regularly speaks of a ‘migrant invasion’ and used Sanchez’s January decree to call for ‘Repatriations, deportations and remigration’. 

Notably, Sánchez’s speech on the steps of La Moncloa (the Spanish prime minister’s residence) put international talking points at the centre of his pitch, contrasting his positions with the those of the right, and particularly US President Donald Trump and Argentinian President Javier Milei:

‘We have strived to build a better world for our fellow citizens and for the rest of humanity,’ he said, ‘supporting Ukraine, the European Union, and the United Nations in their darkest moments. Denouncing genocidal regimes when others remained silent.

‘Fighting tyrants, techno-oligarchs, and speculators who want to destroy the future of our sons and daughters to enlarge their pockets. Doubling our aid to international cooperation while others boasted of cutting it with their chainsaw or on that military altar of 5 per cent of GDP.’

Spain’s voting system

50 days of intense campaigning and negotiation between parties will now follow. These negotiations matter because of Spain’s electoral system. 

Spain uses the D’Hondt method in provincial constituencies, which punishes parties polling in low single figures. Small parties can survive by running together on a joint list, but past attempts have had mixed results. 

Sumar is the largest of these groupings. Despite having no leader, it has launched ‘Frente Amplio’ (the Broad Front) to try to pull support together. Much will depend on the firebrand MP Gabriel Rufián. He is seen as a potential unifier of the fragmented parties to the left of PSOE. But he is not a Sumar figure, and internal politics and personalities have a habit of wrecking electoral pacts in Spain. Podemos, PSOE’s coalition partner, joined Sumar’s list in 2023 but broke away within months.

For Sánchez, what happens to his left matters more than ever. His pitch therefore needs to be binary. Expect him to use Trump, Milei and Flávio Bolsonaro (ahead in Brazil’s presidential race after the first round) as bogeymen to focus minds even before the ballots are printed.

On the right, the Partido Popular (PP) will likely approach a ‘Ming Vase strategy’ of trying to just get through the next 50 days without any major mishaps. It is not clear that this can work. Questions about what a coalition with Vox would look like will follow their leader Alberto Feijóo. His inability to respond adequately to such questions in 2023 likely cost him victory. 

Spain’s vote will now be the first in a series of crucial European elections. France chooses a new president in spring 2027. Italy, Poland, Finland and Greece are due to vote before the year is out. Many of these contests will look like Spain’s, with some seeing fragile coalitions on the left facing a confident and surging right. 

The results will matter well beyond domestic politics. For instance, as the US continues to demand the continent do more for its own defence, disruptive elections will make it harder to make progress on a more coherent joint European approach to security. This campaign will be closely followed across the continent – and from across the Atlantic – as politicians seek to perfect their pitch in ever more polarized times.

title: Will New Zealand’s election change its foreign policy?
author: jon.wallace
description:
Will New Zealand’s election change its foreign policy? Expert comment jon.wallace 2 November 2026

The current coalition has sought closer relations with the US and rowed back climate commitments. What would change under a coalition of the left?

On 7 November, New Zealanders go to the polls in what looks set to be a closely contested general election. As elsewhere, anxiety about the cost of living has dominated the campaign. 

International affairs tend to feature at the bottom of voter concerns. However, like many US citizens voting in this year’s midterm elections, some New Zealanders blame international events like the war in Iran for the higher costs that are their top priority. 

New Zealand’s foreign policy is therefore at stake in this election. And a change of government could substantially reshape the country’s position on key issues.

The foreign policy reset

Since 1996, New Zealanders have voted in a Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) system which normally produces a coalition government.

In 2023, New Zealand formed its first three-party coalition government under MMP. The centre-right National Party, led by Christopher Luxon, was joined by the right-libertarian Act Party and right-wing populist New Zealand First Party, led by Winston Peters. Peters took on the role of foreign minister – a role he had held twice before.

As a small, open, Pacific economy, recent New Zealand governments have generally sought balance in foreign policy. On the one hand they have nurtured the increasingly important trade relationship with China, building on a long history of openness to engagement with Beijing (China has been New Zealand’s largest trading partner since 2017).  On the other hand, governments have sought security and other partnerships with the US and other IP4 countries like Japan, Australia and South Korea. 

However, after the 2023 election the coalition announced a ‘reset’ in foreign policy, aligning New Zealand more closely with the US and Australia.

This has not meant total alignment with Washington. The coalition has supported Ukraine against Russia’s war of aggression. It has stressed the importance of free maritime movement, including in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait. And it has stated its support for the international justice system.

But the government has also expressed interest in joining AUKUS Pillar II – an Australia–UK–US security initiative – and deepened military cooperation with the US. It has near-doubled defence spending, while weakening engagement on humanitarian issues and climate security. 

Meanwhile, relations with China have cooled. China has shifted to making public comments on New Zealand’s foreign policy – particularly its AUKUS discussions. And in May Beijing imposed travel bans on New Zealand MPs that visited Taiwan, something that New Zealand politicians have done without consequence since 1972.

Seeking a closer relationship with Washington, the coalition has maintained a ‘softly-softly’ approach to the dramatic changes in foreign policy during the second Trump administration. Wellington’s response to US pressure on Canada, Mexico and Denmark – and the multilateral system in general – has been muted. And, though government policy is to support a Two-State Solution, the conflict in Gaza and the US-Israeli war against Iran have exposed foreign policy faultlines.

In 2025, New Zealand declined to recognize Palestinian statehood, diverging from partners like Australia, the UK, Canada and France. In March, released emails showed Prime Minister Luxon wanted to show ‘explicit public support’ for the US war against Iran.

But closer security alignment with Washington has not exempted New Zealand from a higher 12.5 per cent rate of US tariffs, leading to a 13 per cent decrease in exports to the US in the first year. And it has not shielded the country from the impact of the US–Iran war. Many New Zealanders blame these factors for increasing prices at home – as do some coalition government ministers.  

What a change in government might mean

Crucially, New Zealand’s reset was not put to voters at the last election in 2023. This time, some parties have set out some foreign policy positions in advance. 

The Labour Party pledged in 2024 not to join AUKUS Pillar II. And the party says it would recognize Palestine statehood and enforce sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. 

The National Party, meanwhile, has pledged to continue to invest in defence, seek new trade relationships, and boost the medicine budget of the government’s pharmaceutical agency by cutting foreign aid outside of the Pacific. 

Climate is the area of greatest division. The coalition’s interventionist approach against climate litigators risks leaving New Zealand in breach of its climate obligations. That could threaten its trade relationship with the EU. In contrast, parties like Labour promise to prioritize compliance with climate commitments and relationships with the EU, as well as Canada and ASEAN. Labour also says it would express greater support for multilateral institutions like the World Health Organization (WHO). (Under the current coalition, New Zealand has abstained from or rejected significant global health measures).

Labour has been the most proactive about publicising foreign policy commitments in its election campaign. But a clear strategy from either of the largest parties is still lacking. The stances of smaller parties, who will serve as coalition partners, are even more opaque. 

Power favouritism increases vulnerability 

Throughout the campaign, polling has shown a finely balanced race. A small percentage of undecided voters could yet install a left-wing coalition led by the Labour Party – or maintain the status quo. 

Related work

New Zealand should rethink its pivot towards the US to retain strategic autonomy in the Indo-Pacific

Were the coalition re-elected, New Zealand’s foreign policy would likely extend the first term’s agenda. Peters would probably remain in post as foreign minister. And the relationship with China will continue to be delicate, especially following recent events. In July, Peters directed remarks at a left-wing Chinese-New Zealander in Parliament that were condemned as racist at home and prompted a formal protest by Beijing. 

The pursuit of positive US relations would also probably continue under any new government. But it will need to be refined. 

The policy is predicated on the belief that Washington is a reliable security partner in the Indo-Pacific. But US attention is fixed on the Middle East and its commitment to its alliances less sure than ever – leaving New Zealand potentially vulnerable. 

Europe and the IP4 have acknowledged the need for enhanced Pacific security engagement to compensate. But the US will still need to be involved to counter China’s influence in the region. The challenge is to engage Washington without relying exclusively on it.

Informed consent at the ballot-box

As a small economy, New Zealand is more vulnerable to shocks. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the war in Iran have contributed to higher inflation, trade disruption, and a weaker New Zealand dollar. 

It can help New Zealand to retain a level of strategic ambiguity in its foreign policy. But this must be balanced with the right of voters to have their say in how the country positions itself and understand the trade-offs involved. 

To ensure that voters can make informed decisions, political parties need to be clearer about their foreign policy positions. Parties should define the principles and red lines they will use to guide relations with the US and China, spell out their positions on security alliances, and more clearly articulate what they see as New Zealand’s role in the Pacific.

These positions need not be fixed or undermine strategic ambiguity. But parties should outline their policies clearly enough for voters to evaluate them. If either party believes another ‘reset’ in foreign policy is necessary, they should make an argument for it and win New Zealanders’ consent at the ballot box.

title: The war is pushing Iran closer to Russia
author: thilton.drupal
description:
The war is pushing Iran closer to Russia Expert comment thilton.drupal 2 November 2026

A flurry of diplomatic meetings and positive statements suggest Tehran sees closer cooperation with Moscow as key to its short-term survival and long-term deterrence.

The US-Israeli war with Iran is fundamentally changing how Tehran views Russia. Moscow was previously perceived by some in Tehran as an unreliable partner that benefited disproportionately from Iran’s support. But Russia is now increasingly seen as an important partner to ensure Iran’s military survival, post-war reconstruction and long-term deterrence. 

Positive meetings

In October alone, senior Iranian and Russian officials held three high-level meetings, reflecting the growing importance both governments attach to the partnership. 

On 8 October, Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian met Russian president Vladimir Putin in Turkmenistan on the sidelines of regional summit meetings. They emphasized the mutual political will to deepen ties across virtually every sector, including trade and economic cooperation.

On 19 October, Russia’s foreign minister Sergei Lavrov travelled to Tehran for the first since the war began on 28 February. He met President Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Supreme National Security Council head Mohsen Rezaei. They discussed energy, transport and broader bilateral relations. The meetings emphasized the need to advance the comprehensive strategic partnership signed in January 2025, continuing economic and investment cooperation despite the challenges posed by the war.

Related work

Russia–Africa Summit: Moscow is engaging more with Africa, but its delivery is limited

After the meetings, Araghchi stated: ‘never in our history have Iran and Russia worked as closely as now.’ Pezeshkian thanked Russia for its support during the war. Security chief Rezaei also emphasized Tehran’s determination to strengthen strategic cooperation with Moscow, indicating that Iran’s security leadership also supports closer relations. 

On 27 October, Pezeshkian visited Moscow to attend the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, where he again held talks on bilateral cooperation with Putin. Pezeshkian thanked Putin for ‘backing and assistance’ in both political and economic matters. Putin said that bilateral trade increased by 10.4 per cent during the first eight months of 2026.

Putin also reaffirmed Moscow’s commitment to ongoing projects, including the Bushehr nuclear power plant. Russia’s state-owned nuclear corporation, Rosatom, announced it would increase the number of its construction workers at Bushehr to 200. Rosatom had evacuated its staff after the outbreak of the war. 

Outside of this nuclear development, the substance of these meetings was not significantly different to previous high-level exchanges. What stands out, however, is the increasingly positive tone of public statements by senior figures across Iran’s political and security establishment. This suggests a more favourable assessment of Russia’s strategic value, although it does not necessarily indicate a fundamental change in the views of all Iranian decisionmakers.

Moving beyond scepticism

This enthusiasm contrasts with earlier doubts within Tehran about the benefits of investing in Moscow as an ally. Elements of the Iranian leadership have long held a deep-seated scepticism towards Russia. 

This scepticism had grown since late 2022 as some in Tehran questioned the returns on its support for Russia’s war in Ukraine. Iran has supplied Russia with thousands of drones, including Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 models, along with other military assistance. Iran has publicly denied involvement in the conflict, but admitted it had sent drones to Russia before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and Iranian officials told Reuters months into the war that Tehran had agreed to supply more drones and missiles. 

Leaked contract documents indicate that Russia agreed to pay approximately $290,000 per drone for a bulk purchase of 2,000 Shahed-136 drones, although the extent to which these payments were completed remains unclear. Iran has also reportedly helped to establish production facilities in Russia, enabling Moscow to domestically manufacture a modified version of Iran’s Shahed-136 drone named Geran-2. 

However, influential voices in Tehran have often questioned the strategic alliance with Moscow. One former IRGC naval commander said ‘There is a view that Russia sought to drag Iran into that [Ukraine] war … so it would not be alone and the pressure of sanctions would increase on Iran.’ In 2022, the US and EU imposed additional sanctions on Iran over its sales of drones to Russia. During Lavrov’s previous visit to Tehran in February 2025, Iranian commentators warned that Moscow might use Iran as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Washington over Ukraine. 

Critics of closer relations have also argued that Russia was benefiting disproportionately from Tehran’s support, without providing comparable assistance in return. In particular, Tehran felt Russia did not significantly come to its aid during the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025. Russia failed to deliver advanced weapons systems that Iran said it had purchased before the war, such as SU-35 fighter jets.

Support for closer cooperation

The US-Israeli war appears to have prompted a reassessment of Russia’s value to Tehran. According to several reports, Russia provided Iran with intelligence on US military positions, satellite imagery for targeting, and weapons components. It is difficult to assess the real battlefield impact of Russian support. However, despite President Donald Trump’s statement that Moscow and Beijing have not been helping Tehran, the evidence suggests otherwise.

Such support is likely to have strengthened the position of those within Iran’s security establishment who have long advocated closer ties with Moscow. For this group, who were supported by the late former president, Ebrahim Raisi, the war has vindicated their longstanding argument that closer cooperation with Russia could deliver tangible strategic benefits. These include helping Iran circumvent sanctions, overcoming diplomatic isolation and countering Western pressure. 

The increasingly positive statements from senior political officials such as Pezeshkian and Araghchi suggests that support for closer cooperation with Russia is becoming more widespread across the Iranian political spectrum, including among those once sceptical of close alignment with Moscow.  

As Tehran prioritizes military survival, deterrence, and reconstruction in the coming months, closer cooperation with Russia will likely be increasingly seen as a strategic necessity rather than merely as a means of circumventing sanctions and resisting Western pressure. The partnership is acquiring a more immediate security rationale, serving both Iran’s current military requirements and its longer-term strategic objectives.

Consequences

In the short term, technical assistance and weapons components could help Iran withstand the conflict by sustaining capabilities degraded by months of fighting. Russian expertise could help Tehran rebuild its air defences, missile infrastructure, and defence industry. Russian intelligence could help Iranian forces track US military assets and inform operational decisions. 

Russian support will be particularly valuable in the event of renewed military escalation. It could improve Iran’s ability to anticipate attacks, preserve its military capabilities and impose costs on its adversaries. However, it is unlikely to fundamentally alter the balance of power in Iran’s favour.

In the medium term, assuming the war comes to an end, Iran-Russia cooperation will likely continue with the aim of rebuilding Iran’s military capabilities. This would likely focus on air defence, drones and missile technology. 

While Russia’s capacity to meet Iran’s demands will remain constrained by its war in Ukraine and pressure on its defence industry, even selective transfers of technology and expertise would help Tehran address its vulnerabilities and accelerate the restoration of its deterrent capabilities. For example, Russia could provide replacement components for the S-300 missile defence system as well as electronic warfare technology.

In the longer term, the most consequential outcome could be the institutionalization of military cooperation between Iran and Russia. Iranian policymakers will remain wary of Russia’s tendency to prioritize its own interests and the absence of a binding security guarantee. But the relationship is likely to become increasingly central in future military planning, procurement and defence-industrial cooperation. This will likely increase Iran’s ability to withstand US military and economic pressure, albeit without being a game changer in the balance of power.

The war may not have transformed Russia into a reliable security guarantor for Iran, but it could make Moscow a more enduring component of Tehran’s security strategy. This will ensure the partnership is harder to reverse, no matter who is in power.

description: Europe’s innovation gap with the US and China lies in breakthrough rather than incremental innovation. This column argues that part of the explanation is the labour market. Breakthroughs come from risky experimentation and experiments often fail and cost workers their jobs. When job loss is costly, workers demand a wage premium to join risky young firms, and that premium acts as a tax on experimentation. Combining a new model, Danish matched employer–employee data and a randomised survey experiment, the authors show that more fluid labour markets lower this premium, raise experimentation, and lift aggregate productivity.

title: Coming of age under populists: The zero-sum legacy of populist rule
author: Nicolas Ajzenman, Cevat Giray Aksoy, Harry Pickard
description: Populist governments are known to leave lasting economic and institutional scars. This column examines a less visible legacy: whether growing up under populist rule changes how citizens see the world. Combining data on populist leaders with surveys of more than 260,000 people in 53 countries, it shows that people exposed to populist governments during early adulthood develop more zero-sum views for around two decades. This is more consistent with a rhetorical channel than with an explanation based on economic hardship.

title: How Well do Bug Bounties Work?
description:
For three decades years, software makers have paid bug bounty hunters to break their code so they can make it more secure. Recently, some software companies have decided that bug bounties programmes aren't useful any more: Curl shut its bounty in January, and Intel suspended its own in September. And the discovery of the PHP flaw that sent websites offline in October came from researchers working with AI, not from a bounty hunter's report.

Tobias Kretschmer (Imperial College London, CEPR) and his co-authors followed 86 programmes on Bugcrowd to discover how they work best. Do you run closed programmes, open only to invited hackers, or open them to all comers? And what happens now that AI is making a bug report cheaper to produce? Tim Phillips asks Kretschmer how well bug bounties are working.
